subtopic: ROSELAND AND OLIVER SUBDIVISIONS, WINDSOR, ONTARIO

speechtext:
Hon. MILTON F. GREGG (Minister of Veterans Affairs): Mr. Speaker, in response to the question submitted yesterday by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), with your permission I would like to make a statement on the Roseland and Oliver subdivisions of the Veterans Land Act, located near Windsor.
Perhaps hon. members might bear with me if I review briefly the history of these subdivisions.
Early in the war it was realized by my predecessor that as a result of high priority wartime expansion of industry, there was likely to develop in Canada a housing shortage and that those likely to be most seriously affected by the shortage would be the veterans
overseas. Accordingly plans were made to meet some of this anticipated shortage under the terms of the Veterans Land Act, and in 1945 construction was commenced on about 2.700 houses across Canada. One hundred of these were located outside the city of Windsor on the Oliver and Roseland subdivisions.
As had been anticipated when the men came back from overseas, there was a very serious shortage of veterans housing in Canada. The Windsor subdivisions were available for occupation in the summer of 1946, and although we realized there were some deficiencies in the houses, we felt that rather than deny the veterans in that area shelter, we should allot the homes as soon as they were reasonably ready for occupancy. About June 1946 the veterans started to move in. They had examined the houses, but we were not at that time in a position to tell them what the final price would be. Accordingly agreements to purchase were not asked at that time, although veterans did sign applications and the majority of them made a deposit of $600.
After the veterans had been in occupation for some time, defects which are inevitable in all immediate postwar construction became apparent. I would ask hon. members to bear in mind in assessing these defects that the director of the Veterans Land Act built these homes during one of the most critical building periods in Canada's history. Material was in very short supply and much of it was not of the quality we would normally have wanted. Skilled labour was equally scarce. When the defects became apparent, my predecessor said on the floor of the house that the houses would be placed in first class condition at no cost to the veteran. That undertaking is being carried out. The majority of the repairs have been completed, but there remain a few things still to be done. I can assure the house, however, that there will be no skimping on any of this necessary remedial work.
In the summer of 1947 we were in a position to inform the veterans what their homes would cost. These prices were not acceptable to the veterans and they refused to sign their agreements to purchase. As a result of this, the deputy minister of the Department of Veterans Affairs, the director of the Veterans Land Act and other departmental officials, met with the veterans in Windsor last fall. They gave most sympathetic consideration to the complaints which were voiced.
Veterans Affairs

The main difference between the department and the veterans was on a matter of price, because by that time it had become apparent that the department intended to live up one hundred per cent to its undertaking to put the houses in first class shape. The veterans at this time pressed for an independent committee to appraise the value of the houses. My predecessor in this portfolio agreed that this should be done. It was his wish that no veteran should be compelled to sign an agreement to purchase a house which did not represent fair value, and he agreed that the only way to make sure that values were equitable and fair was to appoint a committee of independent experts.
In the fall of 1947 the committee was appointed. I would like hon. members to pay particular attention to the names of the men who comprised that committee. It was headed, first of all, by Mr. J. L. B. Price, a man who through the Canadian Legion has long been identified with veterans work. Mr. Price in private life is one of Canada's outstanding building contractors. As a member of the legion he headed the national committee on veterans housing. He has devoted long hours trying to help veterans from one end of Canada to the other with their housing difficulties.
The second member of the committee was Mr. Malcolm D. MacPhail, a very highly regarded Windsor real estate man who has had many years of experience as a valuator. The third man was Mr. Frederick R. Larkin, mortgage supervisor of the London Life Insurance Company at Windsor. These men in my opinion were unusually qualified to pass on real estate values in the area in which these subdivisions are located.
The committee presented their finding to the department on December 18, 1947. I now table the report. Briefly their finding was that in 54 cases the prices which they set on the houses were below the prices which had previously been quoted by the department. In four cases the price they set was the same as that of the department, and in 42 cases their findings show that the value of the houses as fixed by the independent appraisal committee was above the price quoted by the department to the veteran.
I want to make it absolutely clear that this independent appraisal committee set their prices without any reference to the prices previously quoted by the Veterans Land Act administration. They did not have in their possession the prices which the veterans had originally been asked for the houses.

The department has accepted their report in full with the one notable exception. Where the department price has been found to be below that set by the independent committee, the price to the veteran remains the same. Where the appraisal committee's report of values is below the price set by the department, the lower price is being charged.
The price reductions range from a low of .814.03 to a high of $685.71. The total decrease across the two subdivisions is S24,581 out of a total original capital expenditure on this project of 1694,490 78.
I should inform the house that in living up to our undertaking to put these properties in first class shape we are expending a total of 886,004 in remedial repairs. In addition to this, the contractor has accepted responsibility for certain extensive remedial work which is being done at no expense to the public. There, of course, will be no charge against the veteran for any of this work.
I should emphasize, too, that the original price quoted to the veteran was the exact cost of these properties to the director of the Veterans Land Act. It means in effect that in the remedial repairs and the present reduction a total of $110,000 approximately has been spent on these properties to ensure that the veteran is getting maximum value for his money.
To bring the house up to date on: the situation, I may say that a meeting was held with the veterans on Sunday last at which the district superintendent announced to the veterans the present prices on their houses. These prices were not acceptable and a demand has been made for a further downward revision.
I am informed that at Sunday's meeting the veterans went on record unanimously as being completely satisfied with the progress and the quality of the repair program. There were still, it is true, a few minor complaints. But in the main I can assure the house that the veterans are satisfied with the quality and that the one remaining point at issue is the matter of price. That this is true is best evidenced by the fact that when the president of the veterans committee asked for a show of hands from those veterans who intend to purchase their houses, all but two expressed their intention of doing so. I am advised that the two who did not raise their hands included the president of the committee who is planning to build his own house under veterans individual housing.
So we now have a situation where apparently the veterans are satisfied with the conditions of their homes; they are satisfied that the department will complete the remedial pro-

Veterans Affairs
gram in a way acceptable to them. We have prices set not by the department but by an independent appraisal committee as requested by the veterans themselves, but we still have the veterans refusing to accept these prices.
The one request which was made to the veterans at Sunday's meeting was that they let the department know whether they are prepared to sign a purchase agreement or whether they want to go on a temporary rental agreement basis, pending sale to another qualified veteran.
I think hon. members will realize that we must bring this situation to a conclusion. There are at present approximately 250 veterans in Windsor qualified under the Veterans Land Act who have not yet been able to find a home. Further, the house should note that of the 2,673 houses constructed on subdivisions throughout Canada, 2,372 veterans have signed their purchase agreements and furthermore are meeting their payments satisfactorily.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, of which I have given him notice. In view of disturbing reports that embargoes on oil exports, including shipments to Canada, may ba* imposed by the United States, can the minister inform the house whether the matter has been discussed with United States authorities, and what steps he proposes to take if necessary to protect the interests of Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: REPORTED UNITED STATES EMBARGO ON FUEL OIL EXPORTS
speechtext:
The government has for some weeks been concerned with suggestions

that an embargo be imposed on the export of petroleum products from the United States to Canada. Our ambassador at Washington has held frequent conferences with the United States officials in that regard, and officers of their department of commerce have visited Canada to study our position. Our stock position of petroleum products has been fully disclosed. Our steps taken to limit the installation of oil burners throughout 1947 have been explained. After consultation with the petroleum industry in Canada, the government voluntarily has cut imports of petroleum products from United States during January to 50 per cent of quantities imported in the same month a year ago. A corresponding cut is being studied for the months of February and March.
Any embargo on shipments of petroleum products from our traditional source of supply would be a calamity of the first order, but hon. members will appreciate that the decision is for the United States government.

speechtext:
While the name "baby bonus"
is commonly used in reference to social security payments which are made by the government, I presume the hon. gentleman refers to the family allowance. Family allowances are not taxable. People are forced to take the family allowance so that the exemptions of $100 per recipient of those who get the allowance and $300 for those between the age of those receiving the allowance and twenty-one years may be deductible. Anyone who is entitled to the allowance but who does not take it is allowed an exemption
of only $100. That is the reason the plan was adopted of having everybody who had children within the age limit receive the allowance in order that the two different exemptions would be adaptable. The answer to the question is that family allowances are not taxable.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, two months have elapsed since the fateful radio talk of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) on November 17 last when these import conservation regulations were put into effect. subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
The bill is now before us in parliament and we are being asked to pass it. The house is entitled to know what have been the results of these regulations up to date.
In December last the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) asked for certain information and certain statements as to the imports into Canada from the United States in the months just preceding November. Since we are now in this very unusual situation of having these regulations in force since November last, and we are now in January endeavouring to deal with the bill which will enact these regulations into law, it is my purpose to ask the minister to tell the house at this time -because this is the time when we should know it-what have been the results. What United States dollars did we save in the month of November? What United States dollars did we save in December, and what have we saved in January? We are not capable of dealing with this measure, and we should not be asked to deal with it, until we have been told what these results have been.
I see by a press clipping that yesterday the new Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) gave to the people of Toronto some indication of what has been going on. This is the place where the statement should have been made. I am not blaming the minister. Perhaps the timing was wrong; but I am saying to him now that we should like him to elucidate in dollars and cents, not in general terms, what the situation is. For instance, the minister is quoted as saying yesterday:
The program to correct Canada's trade deficiency with the United States is making substantial progress. And I can go farther and say our balance of payment for December was more favourable than was hoped for.
What I am saying, of course, is, let us have the figures. After all, a board of directors of a company would not pass on a matter that had to do with the company unless they had

the information required, and we should not deal with a matter which has to do with the life and death of this country until we have the information asked for. We are being asked to make the stream run backwards, and we want to know why; we want the figures.
In addition we should like to know something about the principle of these schedules. For instance, they have been in force since November 17 last, and from day to day and from week to week changes have been made which we have read about in the press. As members of parliament we have some responsibility in respect to these matters. One of the things that bothers me is this complete and absolute prohibition upon fresh vegetables. I do not want to suggest that the people of Canada are going to have scurvy if they do not get fresh vegetables, but the fact of the matter is that you put the restrictions on and you made them stick right from the word go. In fact you do not say to the people who are subservient to your control, what you propose to do. Has the minister any recommendation or direction to give to the people of Canada or to the producers? Does he intend the growers to get busy and produce leafy vegetables and fresh vegetables for next fall and winter? Does he expect the producers of Canada to go into the business of greenhouse growing of vegetables? Does he expect them to spend their money in providing apparatus and equipment for that purpose? Does he expect the cold storage people to set up plant to deal with this situation? I know he is going to say that it is a short term policy; but how short, or how long? What knowledge have the people of Canada of the preparations that should be made for the future?
The produce dealers have a complaint with the minister. The minister may disagree with them; nevertheless they are in the produce business and he is not. Mr. Robinson, who is secretary treasurer of the Ontario Vegetable and Fruit Growers' Association, had this to say in Toronto on January 21:
Mr. Robinson suggested present high prices had been the result of scarcity that might have been avoided if producers had known in advance that restrictions on United States vegetable imports were planned.
I think he is right ini that. We are still in the valley of indecision and uncertainty. It is the minister's responsibility to tell the producers, the growers and the people what they may expect in the months to come.
I am dealing only with the principle of schedule I. As a matter of fact diamonds and precious stones were in this list but now

The press has referred to "this grave new world" that has been created by these import restrictions. We have it from the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) that many industries must change their program and a few persons must change their employment. That is an important statement.
I am sure that those who are interested in labour will -want to know more about that, and when we are dealing with the principle of the bill we should know it. When the minister says that a few may have to change their employment I do not think he can take offence at me when I remind him that he spoke of "months" a short time ago in dealing with controls and it turned out that he meant not less than a year. In the same way, I feel that labour will want to know what "few" means. Does it mean that we are going back to the days of national selective service when a man could be taken from one sort of employment and put in another? Does it mean that if an industry has to gear itself for the production of new materials, which it was not engaged in before, and1 the men are not capable of doing that type of work, the government will displace them and put them in some other industry? That is something on which we must have some information when we are dealing with the principle of the bill.
Under schedule III of the bill-

I might also refer to a press clipping that comes from the Toronto Star of January 2 last:
Manufacturing industries whose operations are adding to Canada's U.S. dollar drain will probably have their allotment of foreign exchange for U.S. purchases sharply cut in 1948, it was learned today.
The government is working on a formula to cover the supplying of exchange to such companies, and this will be released shortly to allow firms to plan their year's programs on the basis of reduced imports from the U.S.
Slated for cuts are those businesses which consume more U.S. dollars for imports than they produce through the sale of their products.

With regard to the austerity program, I am not prepared to say that anyone in this country should go out and tell another that he should tighten his belt in order to conserve American dollars. I am not prepared to say that this measure is going to offer any solution to our Canadian problem. I believe it is creating new problems, that we are losing our sovereignty and that we are giving it over to others for exploitation in the future.
What is the future of steel? I cannot see any possibility of developing it; and I cannot see that possibility because in the United States they are searching for ore. Their ore resources are almost depleted, and we know about the search that is taking place.
In May of 1947 Bill No. 10, letter H of the senate, was passed by this house. Only a few of us questioned it. At that time I was looking to the future so far as the steel situation in eastern Canada is concerned. A clipping I have here from that authoritative journal, the Financial Post, says that there is a possibility of a shift in the United States steel industry. It states:
If the new iron ore deposits in South America and Ungava should prove to be economically feasible, the new discoveries may mean a major shift of United States industry. The whole United States steel industry is located in relation to the Take Superior deposits of iron ore.
The minister is familiar with the ore situation in the United States. Having this in mind, when that bill came before the house, and when the Hollinger-North Shore Exploration Company and the Quebec North Shore and Labrador Railway Company secured franchises from the Canadian government for the purpose of taking over complete control of the ore deposits in that section, I said to myself:	There goes Canada's chance of
developing her own steel industry. Because who are the Hollinger people in Canada? They are linked with the National Steel Corporation of the United States. The Hollinger Consolidated Gold Mines are linked with the National Steel Corporation of the United States and other major United States iron and steel companies, through the M. A. Hanna Company. In 1943 the M. A. Hanna Company acquired a minority interest in the Labrador Mining and Exploration Company. The controlling interest in the Labrador Min-

Mr. Speaker, there are just two subjects I want to deal with. Years ago one of our great leaders, Sir John A. Macdonald, introduced a national policy which has never been changed in principle. The Liberals have always claimed that they were a low tariff party, but they have continually added to that policy. The measure now before us does nothing more than add to that policy. At times many farmers and producers have questioned the wisdom of it, but I believe the people throughout the country realize that we must protect our industries. The late President Roosevelt of the United States introduced what was termed the new deal. I am wondering whether the deal that was introduced here on November 17 will be referred to as the raw deal. I am wondering also if the people are not wishing for a square deal. I hope that that is what we will get in the future.
I am going to deal particularly with the position of the fruit and vegetable growers. For many years these producers have been denied the cream of the Canadian market. As soon as their products were ready to market, or just prior to that time, fruits and vegetables grown in areas where they ripen sooner were allowed to come into the country in large quantities. When complaints were made the answer given was that these were brought
Foreign Exchange Conservation

in and sold before the local products are ready to market. However, in many cases carloads of these early fruits and vegetables were brought in from the United States and stored and our growers had to take a licking.
What is the position of these growers today? They are confused; they are undecided as to just what to do. One group is saying, "Produce to the limit." Another group is saying, "Be careful, be cautious, because by the time you come to harvest your crop your throats will be cut." About the time Canadian peaches were ready to come on the market last year, 300 carloads of Georgia peaches came into this country and were sold in competition with the local product. Ontario and Michigan fruits ripen at practically the same time. But huge quantities of Michigan cherries were admitted into the country just at the time Canadian cherries were coming on the market. The same thing can be said about head lettuce, tomatoes, and practically all other vegetables and fruits that we grow in Canada.
The consumers in the cities are blaming the Canadian growers because certain fruits and vegetables are not available, and they are demanding the removal of some of these restrictions. In one breath they ask for controls, and in the next breath they ask for the removal of restrictions. The importers and the wholesalers are demanding the removal of these restrictions because they do not care about the primary producers. How can the Canadian producer be expected to supply a market overnight which he has been denied for fifteen years or more? On the other hand Canadian farmers are denied a most lucrative United States market for beef, wheat and other farm products.
A couple of sessions ago some questions were asked about the shortage of lumber. The classic answer that was made was that for every carload produced in Ontario and sold domestically another carload was permitted to go to the United States. It was said that because of the high prices that obtained in the United States lumber could be sold more cheaply to Canadians. Why not try out that theory on farm products? Why not let us send our beef and wheat to the United States and see how it will work out? It did not work out that way with lumber, and it will not work out that way with wheat, but in the meantime the Canadian farmer is being euchred out of millions of dollars because he is being deprived of that market. No other group in our economy is being denied that market. Our fishermen, our miners and those who produce forest products all have entry to the United States market where the}' are able

to obtain United States dollars, but not the Canadian farmer. Our farmers would be glad to bring in a few hundred million United States dollars.
What do the fruit and1 vegetable growers actually need? All they ask is that they be given the natural market for the products they can grow in this country. They ask that and no more. They want assurance from this government so that they can go ahead and plan and plant. They want assurance that when they are ready to harvest they will be able to obtain some reward for the investment they have made and the labour they have expended. They want assurance that there will not be a change of heart on the part of this government because of pressure exerted by consumers and importers to have these restrictions removed. They want these assurances right away, because planting time for early vegetables and fruit is fast approaching. Up to the moment the growers have not had that assurance. How are they to know what acreage to plant unless that assurance is given.
I think this measure has developed a lack of confidence in the government. In the first place the program was introduced more or less with an apology. It was said that it was temporary, that it might not last long, and reference was made to months. However, we are not certain whether it will be a hundred months or two months or how long it will be. What assurance is there to industry to go ahead1 and build plants when this is simply a temporary measure to correct an exchange situation. No wonder industry is marking time and following a wait-and-see policy.
Let me give you figures to show what is happening in the city of London, Ontario. Prior to November 17, the number of persons passing through the employment office was fewer than 500 a week. Last week 2,100 passed through that office looking for work.
We hear a lot about the high cost of living, and most of the outcry is against the high prices of food. We do not hear much complaint about the prices of beer or automobiles or refrigerators. The only thing that worries people is, when can I get it? But people generally do complain about the prices of food. They are not complaining about taxes to any great extent, but taxes play a large part in the high cost of living. An increase of 25 per cent in the excise tax on many goods is being imposed. Let us see what taxation does to the cost of living.
I have mentioned that there was a drive by consumers against food prices, the drive being concentrated against food prices and the farmer. According to an article in the Globe

and Mail of January 12, 1948, thirty-three and a third per cent of every dollar earned in Canada, when paid out for goods and services, goes into taxation, in hidden taxes of one kind and another. What does that actually mean to a family in the city of London? The average weekly wage in the city of London is $34.95. Of that amount, $11.66 is made up of taxes. No wonder food prices are high! Actually the money spent on food, clothing and shelter is not $34.95 but $23.29, the remainder, $11.66, going into taxation. No wonder the government has a fictitious surplus of $700 million! That works out at between $55 and $60 taken from every man, woman and child in Canada without reason, and for a family of four persons it means $240. That $240 would buy a lot of butter, beef, bacon and milk. It would help to take care of some of the high cost of living. If it was not taken from the people in taxes it would be easier for them to pay today's prices for butter and milk and bacon and eggs.

I want to endorse what the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) said about the development of our coal resources. At present we are largely dependent on the United States for our coal supply and yet, as he mentioned, in Alberta and the maritimes we
have vast coal resources. After all we did in the war, surely we can do something to develop the coal resources of this country.
Mr. JOHN T. HACKETT (Stanstead): Mr. Speaker, I listened on the night of the 17th of November to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the speech which came to us from London; later I listened with great interest to the speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). Shortly after they had stopped speaking I was asked by a newspaper what I thought of the policy that had been enunciated by the leader of the government and stated in greater detail by my hon. friend. I said, and it appeared in the press next morning, on November 18:
It is a great tragedy that the only two remaining freely trading nations should in peacetime at the instigation of Canada, put up a curtain on their trading relations.
To admit that a country like Canada, whose whole destiny depends on multilateral trade, should suggest restrictions and controls is one of the most humiliating pages in Canadian history. It reveals the desperation of a government incapable of high policy.
Possibly' if I had had a little more time I might have expressed the same thought in language a little more temperate. However, that was my opinion, and whether it be good or bad it is one that I retain and one that has been fortified by the events which have taken place since these two remarkable utterances.
I ask hon. gentlemen to take a general view of the situation which confronted the Minister of Finance on the day of his pronouncement. Some two and a half years had elapsed since the end of hostilities. I am one of those who believed in 1945 and said then that the wise policy for the government to follow after the cessation of hostilities was to do away with all the controls which had been introduced as a war measure and which we had borne during the period of the war for the purpose of winning the war. Two and a half years have gone by but controls are still with us. By extraordinary means we revived, a little while before the war, the War Measures Act, chapter 206 of the Revised Statutes of Canada. The National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, chapter 25 of the statutes of 1945, was enacted on December 18, 1945. A few months later it was extended by chapter 60 of the statutes of 1946. Then we passed the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act, 1947, which became effective on May 1, 1947; and last autumn we passed a measure which made controls operative until the end of March. 1948. We are confronted now with this Bill No. 3 and I am as certain as I am
Foreign Exchange Conservation

that I stand in my place that more legislation continuing controls will confront us before the end) of this session.
I ask the minister, what have controls given us? Immediately after the end of the war we were told that we did not want the high prices which followed the first great war. If the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) were here he w'ould recall that he took occasion-and others about him joined in-to chide me because I said something about butter going to seventy cents a pound; that I did not consider it would be a great tragedy if for once that element of our community who made butter, the farmers, shared in the so-called prosperity that had resulted from the war. What have all these controls given us? We know' that there were high prices after the first great war. But I put it to hon. gentlemen, two and a half years after the first great war was there the same confusion,; was there the same disturbance in all realms of national activity that wre find today? Were people frustrated, and was government enmeshed, despondent and helpless as it is today? As a result of controls we have had shortages, strikes, high cost of living, inflation, inader-quate production and, finally, what? More controls. Is that not a fair statement? Is that not a fair recapitulation of the story of the last two and a half years?
I understand that the minister was very much disturbed by the rapid disappearance of United States dollars which are required for the purchase in the United States of some things essential and some things that may not be quite so essential. The hon. member for Oape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), who spoke this afternoon, made some reference to the inadequacy of Canada's supply of fuel, that coal and oil are not in as abundant supply here as in some other countries. That, unfortunately, is true; yet we have here something that is called white coal. We have vast quantities of hydro-electric power, which is still in the process of being developed and which in a large measure is a substitute for fuel. Our sources of hydro electric energy have not yet been fully exploited, and they to a large extent could replace the shortage to which the hon. member for Cape Breton South has referred. I say with him-and it has not often been my good fortune to agree with him-that if I thought this bill would achieve the purpose which the minister says he believes it will achieve I would oppose it with some regret, though I would still oppose it, because there is in the bill a kernel of error, a fundamental wrongness which cannot be cured.

Let us look at our present situation. We are told that we have inflation. That means, to put it very simply, that there is more purchasing power, there is more money about than there are goods available for purchase. The result is high prices. That is the crying trouble of the hour. It was in an effort to cope with the rising cost of living, in an effort to prevent foodstuffs from going to higher levels, that controls were re-imposed the other day on butter and meat. Here I open a parenthesis to say that butter has become a very scarce commodity because the policy of the government forced the dairymen, at least of eastern Canada, out of the dairy business, made it impossible for the farmer of the eastern townships to produce butter at a profit, forced him to sell his herds, because the farmers could not afford to feed them; we have seen going across the international boundary into the United States hundreds of thousands of dairy cattle that were required to meet the needs of the Canadian people. That is one of the immediate results of controls. My point is that the crisis which the minister is attempting to meet by Bill No. 3 is a crisis created by the policy of the government; the government, in its effort to manage everybody's business, has failed and caused this crisis.
Look at the record. What has the government done in housing? What has it done in reducing the cost of living? What has it done to benefit the farmer? I will not recite the whole litany of the failure of government policy; it would preclude me from discussing the bill. This bill, having in view the high cost of living, having in view inflation, says what? It says that the Canadian people shall not import from the United States goods which are desired here. It will create a shortage of goods. There will be fewer goods to buy. The result is that the prices of the goods which are available will go up and Canada will have higher prices and more inflation.
I think that is a necessary result if this bill becomes law. And how by the restriction of the importation of capital goods like machinery and steel we can hope to increase production I do not know. We are told on all sides that the solution of our trouble is increased production. We have full employment. How then we shall increase, production by cutting off the supply of capital goods, that is to say the means of increasing our industrial plant and producing capacity, is just something that one of my feeble mentality is unable to grasp. How we can hope to produce more goods when-if we accept the boast of the government-we have, full employment, without an immigration policy, is again a matter I do not understand.

Foreign Exchange Conservation
I say, therefore, that on all these counts the bill introduced by the hon. gentleman will not achieve the purpose which he wishes to achieve by it.
I should like to say a few words on another aspect of the bill. Why is the Canadian dollar incapable of purchasing United States dollars at parity? I think one of the reasons is that Canada has so controlled its finances, has made so insecure the Canadian dollar in the hands of the American, that the American feels that, whatever the inherent value of the dollar, it has been so bedevilled by the controlling agencies in Canada that it is not a safe commodity in which to invest.
We need capital in this country. We have a vast hinterland. We can hope to emerge from the heavy debt that has been imposed upon us by war, and by sundry pastimes in which the government has indulged on the eve of elections, only by the development of our natural resources; andi for that purpose we need capital. We need capital that will come from outside our own economy. We need capital that is willing to gamble on the possibility of success of the venture in which it is engaged, and we have slammed the door in the face of those who would come here and invest in our country.
Why have we done that? We have done that through fear, fear of economic domination. If anybody doubts that, let him turn to the preface of the control act of 1946. The full title of the measure is "An act respecting the control of the acquisition and disposition of foreign currency and the control of transactions involving foreign currency or non-residents." It declares:
Whereas it is desirable to control and protect the value of the Canadian monetary unit in relation to foreign currencies . . . and
Whereas it is desirable to ensure that the said resources in foreign currency are used to promote and facilitate trade and other normal current transactions with other countries and are not dissipated through disadvantageous exports of capital from Canada or for other purposes disadvantageous to Canada as a whole

What that means simply is that the citizens of the United States who have brought their money here in good faith and have put it into the development of our resources are no longer free to take it back as and when they determine proper. The act continues:
. . . to aid in the control and protection of the value of the Canadian monetary unit in relation to foreign currencies and to supervise and control transactions between residents of Canada and residents of other countries which involve or relate to foreign currencies.
That was bad enough. At that level Canada was controlling her dollars on the basis of economics. But today we have descended to another level. We have now come to the
political level, and I assert that this political manipulation of our dollar is one of the most dangerous undertakings that any Canadian government has ever entered upon.
After all, our friends in the United States are people who, like ourselves, do not rejoice in being discriminated against, and if we say to them that we are not going to allow goods which they make come within our territory then they may very properly say that goods which they need at home such as coal, oil, sugar and cotton may not come into Canada. I say that this legislation and other legislation like it, which is essentially political and which is passed for the purpose of securing political favour at this particular time, invites retaliation, misunderstanding, ill will and trouble between the two great peoples of this North American continent.
Now why this Bill No. 3? The Foreign Exchange Control Act confers broad powers upon the government, and yet they are held to be inadequate. When we see the broad powers that are conferred upon the government; when we are told that they no longer suffice; when we turn to the act and read that a minister, w'ithout let or hindrance, is to have the power to rewrite the whole fiscal policy of our country, for no better reason than that he dislikes the colour of somebody's hair, it makes one wonder seriously where the country is going and what has become of parliament itself.
Hon. gentlemen are familiar with the terms of the Foreign Exchange Control Act. It gives the broadest powers. It is effective until March, 1949, an adequate period within which to overcome any little difficulty. But no, the government says it is not sufficient. We find in section 6 of the bill which is before the house at the present time, that the minister is empowered to rewrite any order in council which may have been passed. Here are the terms of the act. Under section 5 the governor in council may make regulations; and one would think the governor in council would be pretty busy if he made regulations for all the possibilities that are set forth in this section 5. But not content with that we have section 6.

Mr. Speaker, I submit I am in order. I am dealing with the principle of the bill. To illustrate how pernicious is the principle of the bill I cite paragraph (c) of section 6, which is in these terms:
(c) in particular cases or classes of cases, from time to time, prescribe terms of, and eondi-

Foreign Exchange Conservation
'tions to a permit or the permission granted in a permit additional to those prescribed by regulation.
This means that the regulations in themselves, as I said a moment ago, may be torn up at any time and completely altered and modified by the right hon. gentleman whose duty it is to administer them. That subsection is inserted for a political purpose. On several occasions I have pointed out that we have become so used to disrespect and perversion of the constitution that we sometimes forget we have one. It is admitted that in cases of emergency like war the normal operation of the constitution is suspended and extraordinary powers may toe assumed by the cabinet. The federal government in such an emergency may even over-ride and supersede provincial jurisdiction. The government has provided emergencies every time we have had political crises. I submit, with the utmost deference, that at the present time there is no emergency whatever. This is merely a political crisis, and to meet it the government is resorting to those methods which were resorted to in the dangers of war. These crises are not peculiar to ourselves. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance does not remember from personal recollection any more than I do, but his birth and sojourn on the border has taught him well that the time was when it took two United States dollars to buy one Canadian dollar. That time went on, not for months but for years. At that time there was no attempt to prevent the purchase in Canada of goods that were just as desperately needed in the United States as United States goods are needed here today. Yet there was no attempt in the United States to meet that political crisis in the way in which we are attempting to meet this political crisis.
I venture the suggestion that this bill is unconstitutional. Somebody may say, "What section of the British North America Act does it contravene?" My answer is that the constitution is not contained in its entirety within that statute. The Canadian constitution is a living thing. It is something that is made up of custom, of tradition and of respect for the way we have lived, worked, prayed, and prospered for seventy or eighty years. It is based upon the respect for a long tradition which emerged from great trials and much bloodshed and which gave to those who came before us that measure of freedom which made Britain looked to and envied by all freedom-loving peoples. Our constitution is not found in its entirety and exclusively within the four corners of that document which was enacted at Westminster in 1867 and which became effective here on the first day of July of that year. That was merely an outline or a char-

ter; it did not by any means contain the whole doctrine, the whole belief, the whole tradition of the constitution that ensured the dignity and freedom of the Canadian citizen.
Just where have we ceased to be constitutional? Canada has a constitutional, representative, responsible form of government; and here we find legislation brought in which is nothing more than a laissez passer. This house has been asked to say that the right hon. gentleman, the minister-what is he minister of now?

speechtext:
The right hon. gentleman who was minister of reconstruction is now under Bill No. 3 to be able to re-write the tariff legislation of this country as many times a day as he wishes and he is to be able to determine who is entitled to favour and who is not. Paragraph (c) reads:
In particular cases or classes of cases, from time to time, prescribe terms of, and conditions to a permit or the permission granted in a permit additional to those prescribed by regulation.
Mr. Speaker, if we were to transfer ourselves to that remote land of Russia and we were dealing with an economic problem, I ask you how could any administrator, how could any gentleman in the position of Mr. Stalin, have more absolute, uncontrolled and irresponsible latitude than this house is asked to confer upon the minister of reconstruction? If that is not unconstitutional; if that is not a perversion; if that is not turning to ridicule the whole theory of parliamentary government, the whole theory of the responsibility of government, then I am sadly mistaken.
I would draw to the attention of the house the fact that the difficulty goes far beyond that. We hear bandied about from time to time the term "bureaucrat". I am not for one moment going to quarrel with the gentlemen who control our economy if this bill become law; but how many times has it happened in this parliament that ministers have come to the house and been absolutely baffled and puzzled and even taken by surprise by orders in council the existence of which they had denied, and which, I believe in all sincerity, they knew nothing about.

How can it be expected that a person, even one with the incomparable energy, talent and ability of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe), can hope in detail to supervise the multifarious trades, deals and negotiations of individual Canadians? Yet he has said that each case has to be dealt with on its merits. That opens the door to all kinds of difficulties and abuses. It means that men who owe no responsibility to parliament are going to write and rewrite every day the tariff laws of the dominion. It means that so long as this legislation is on the statute books we shall be subject to management by men who are not elected by the people of Canada, who owe no duty to the people of Canada, or, so far as that goes, to parliament itself.
In my submission this is utterly and completely unconstitutional. It is a tearing asunder; it is a disruption and destruction of the constitution; it is the bringing into existence of another and new method of managing the affairs of the country. It is putting the people of Canada back under the yoke of controls, making parliamentary control farcical and futile.
I ask the Minister why he goes on with this bill. What lasting benefits does he expect Canada to derive from it? Can he turn to any country at any time in the history of humanity in which a group of men, good and talented as they may be-to say nothing of a single individual-has ever been able to manage successfully the affairs of a whole people? I admonish the government that for their own comfort in debate it would do well to keep away from the historical argument, because it points to the conclusion that men should not be so self-confident about their ability to plan. The general record of. mankind has been- one of great poverty, and by far the most fruitful method1 ever stumbled upon to make the world richer has been that of leaving men free, within the limits of criminal and1 civil law, and letting them engage their energies on their own account and for their own reward. This was discovered against all the instincts and traditions of kings and other rulers who found it very much against their grain to leave the public any part of the management df their own trade, manufacturing or finance.
We have never in the long story of mankind found these tactics leading anywhere but to tyranny. This is a misconceived policy. We have enjoyed liberty so long that we have forgotten its price. We have put physical comfort and material advantage on a higher plane than they should be. We have made money more important than men. We have
forgotten the importance of liberty; we have scorned the spiritual condition of freedom, and we are asked in this bill to sacrifice both to a very fleeting, futile and doubtful advantage.

Here we have before us perhaps the most important measure which will be brought before the House of Commons this session. It is more important than any other measure which will come before us.
While I am not disturbed by the small number of government members who sat in the house yesterday and who are here again today-because I realize they will not do as I tell them, and perhaps will not listen too attentively anyway-the peculiar fact is that, despite the importance of this measure, not one private member on the government side of the house has stood up to give it his endorsation.

This is the sounding board for members of parliament. This is the place ini which one expects them to give to the house and the government some idea as to the grievances the people have, some idea of the people's reaction to the various measures the government has passed or is proposing.
So I say that none of the private members on the government side has yet risen in his place to endorse this measure. However, the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. McCubbin) does not agree with this; he is opposed to it. Recently, speaking in the town of Hensall he said, according to a newspaper article, he irked at new controls. The article states that the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture went on to deplore the fact that he had picked up the paper that morning and found that the government was putting back controls. And he went on to say:
Because I represent farmers and am speaking in a riding just like my own, I want to say I will do my best to see the government puts price ceilings on the things that the farmer has to

buy. I know the Liberal government is certainly not going to see the farmers singled out and left without protection.
If ceilings are put on what the farmer has to sell then I feel sure he is going to get a fail-deal when he goes into the buying market.
Where is that voice now? Has that voice been raised on the other side of the house urging the government to do those things which he thought ought to be done? As parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture he holds a responsible position and he should be using his influence and voice to see that, those things are done which will be in the best interests of the farmers.
We must realize that for a long time we have been living in a fool's paradise. We have not faced facts. The government has never been frank and honest with the people in giving them facts. How well do we remember that prior to his going overseas the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) spoke in Toronto and gave an interview to the press. There never was a more optimistic interview given to the press then the one he gave at that time. He said there would be no depression in Canada, that there was no danger of these austerities which might come as a result of these things. Then he left for the old country on what was to be just a little trip, nothing of any great importance. He came back and went to Washington and that is when the trouble started. That is where the schemes that we are questioning today were formulated.

speechtext:
Never once since the end of the war two and a half years ago has this government taken the people of this country into its confidence and told them the things that it ought to have told them. During the war we appealed to the people of this country to support the government in its war measures. The people of Canada showed that they were prepared in times of peace to do everything necessary to rehabilitate and reconstruct this country, to keep our industries going, to make it the type of country expected by the returned man.
A great deal of work was done by the industries of this country. When the famous white book on reconstruction was got out after a

lengthy survey of the industries across this country, industry generally' co-operated in every possible way to formulate plans along with the government and the department of reconstruction to keep industries going, in order that our people might be gainfully employed and to provide those'things which the people needed and had been without during the war. Where is that white book now? Who ever hears of it? Who ever hears of that planning?
As we have said, the same thing is true all the way through the picture. The post-war planning of this government has been null and void. The government has kept us living in a fool's paradise. We have finally reached the time when the private members of the government will not stand up in this house to endorse this measure. The chickens have come home to roost; the day of action has long passed; the day of reckoning is here.
For many months tariff experts from the different nations of the world sat at Geneva. They put in a lot of hard work in an effort to try' to plan a new world system of trade. I believe in protection and so does everyone else in this house.

It does not matter whether a man belongs to a trade union, he believes in a type of production. The man on the farm believes in a type of production. The industrialist believes in a type of production. The merchant believes in a type of production. Doctors and lawyers are more protectionists than anyone else. Like many thousands of others engaged in industry, like many thousands working in industry, I was looking forward to the day when those Geneva .agreements- would become law. People were prepared to modify their views on protection because they felt that, as a result of these Geneva agreements, we would have more trade in the world and gainful employment would be provided for our people and we would be able to help to rehabilitate the countries which had been devastated by the war.
I said that none of the ministers has been honest with our people. At noon today I heard a man speak and he referred to the frankness which had been shown in Great Britain. How well we remember the words that Churchill used when he told the people that he could promise them only blood, sweat and tears. This gentleman told us how Sir Stafford Cripps had said the other day that the country would have to work to produce. Ever since the end of the war not once have we heard anything in the way of pessimism

______________Foreign Exchange Conservation
from members of the cabinet. This at a time when we should have heard some note of pessimism. The Canadian people should have been made to realize what they would have to go through in the course of months or perhaps years.
Then the famous night came when the Geneva agreements were to be made known to the world. Along with hundreds of thousands of people, perhaps millions, we listened to hear what these Geneva agreements would mean. Here was the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) speaking from London and telling us what was being done. We listened attentively. We could not get all the details, but at first hand we thought that here was something which would be helpful. Perhaps in the working out there would have to be changes made, as is always done with trade agreements, but we felt that this was a start, that here was a large group of nations willing to co-operate on such a vital matter as world trade and the betterment of world conditions.
Then suddenly the Minister of Finance came on the air and the Geneva agreements were nullified then and there. World trade was stopped. I laughed to myself because I realized that hon. gentlemen opposite in some parts of the country have been more free traders than anyone else, and in other parts of the country they have been, high protectionists. They have always labelled us with being the friends of great industry, as being the seekers of high protection; but here was the Minister of Finance, not asking just for higher tariffs, but asking for dictatorial tariff powers which would say to a manufacturer, You cannot bring in anything.
When the minister had finished I began to realize something of the ramifications of what he had said and how it would work out. My wife and I had been sitting there listening to the two speeches, and I said to her, "This means the reimposition of controls. Controls must come back because he is taking away competition. The produce of the farmers and fruit and vegetable growers of this country is no longer in the hands of the producers but in the hands of the canners and the middlemen, in the hands of those who store this produce in great warehouses for months and months. So we immediately saw what would happen. The minister must surely have come to realize, as everyone else does, that there are certain immutable laws of economics and that if you start to interfere with one or two of them you must interfere with them all. If you control one thing you must control everything. If the farmer changes one cog on the binder on his farm he must change them all. It is the same with the law of economics and the
laws of nature. They work very well until man starts to interfere. Trees are grown, for instance, to keep streams running. It is the same with the law of economics. This government has been continually monkeying and fooling with them until it has now brought the country into such a chaotic condition that no one knows where he stands. The minister has now started to reimpose some controls.
But what else did he do? After reading his explanation of his austerity program in the papers next day, I asked myself: Is this a "save Canada" policy or a "save Truman" policy? I just wonder. The government is putting an excise tax on goods that are wholly produced and sold in this country, goods made solely of Canadian material. This tax has so increased prices that these goods are now out of reach of a good many people. The price of an electric stove, for example, immediately shot up from S150 to $185, and increases in the same proportion took place in the price of almost every household requirement in this country. It seemed to me as if there was only one explanation. In order to get the acquiescence of the United States to these restrictions the Minister of Finance had to say to them: We shall put such a heavy excise tax on goods manufactured in this country which ordinarily would compete with your goods moving across the border into Canada that our people will not be able to buy them, or industry produce them, so that when we rescind this austerity program, you can make these goods in your industries in the United States and send them in here, and Canadians can walk the streets.
But there is more than that. We promised -and when I say we I mean this house.-that the men returning from overseas would be looked after when they came back and be provided with homes and with all those things that were necessary to rehabilitate them and get them back into civilian life. And we started a housing policy. Now we find that a twenty-five per cent excise tax has been imposed on refrigerators. There was a time when a refrigerator was looked upon as a luxury, and perhaps even today in some old-fashioned homes a refrigerator, if we have to have these austerity measures, may still be looked upon as something of a luxury. But on the other hand we have built thousands of homes across this country for the veterans, and in spite of all we did to force the government to build for the veterans decent homes with cellars under them, many of these homes have no cellars today, and to the veteran living in one of these homes without a cellar a refrigerator is just as necessary as any other piece of furniture. Yet the government says

to him: You cannot have a refrigerator unless you are willing to pay twenty-five per cent more for it, unless you are willing to pay $375 for a $300 refrigerator. That is the situation we have today.
Last night the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), in speaking to the construction association, is reported in this morning's Globe and Mail to have said that profiteering is the one great curse in this country, and that it was the one thing which would break down our economy and private enterprise. Here on the one hand we have the Minister of Labour condemning profiteering, and on the other we have the Minister of Finance making profiteering possible by his controls and the like which are upsetting the whole economic machinery of this country.
And now what are we to have? We are to have a czar in charge of industry. I do not question any man's desire to be fair and honest in the administration of the powers entrusted to him; but, as the hon. member who has just sat down has very well said, it is impossible for any human being to administer such a bill as this and be fair and impartial throughout the whole of his administration.
What happened when the austerity program was announced to the people of this country? Immediately industry started to get worried. Many of them approached me and asked what they should do. I told them to wait, to be patient and see how this thing worked out. I said perhaps the government knows what it is doing; but if it does it is the first time it ever did. So we waited for some days, but no clarification was forthcoming and chaos became worse and worse. We found that the furniture industry, for example, was told that it could not bring in veneers; the textile industry was told that it could not bring in certain cottons that we cannot make in Canada, and other industries found themselves in similar difficulties. Those difficulties have not yet been overcome. Those industries are still waiting and worrying about what is to be done. Do the members of this house representing the various constituencies have to come to Ottawa on behalf of the industries in their ridings and personally interview the new czar we are creating by this bill, or is this to be done by the industries themselves writing in? Just how is this thing going to work? Already I find that some decisions are being made. According to a report in the Brantford Expositor there is an industry there which makes golf clubs, golf balls, squash racquets, tennis racquets, curling paraphernalia and other sporting goods, and according to this newspaper report that industry thanks their member for intervening with the government 
and having the excise tax taken off the sporting goods made in that city, while the tax of twenty-five per cent is still retained on the refrigerators which the veterans of this country need.
My contention is that the time has come when hon. members must take a stand. It is all very well for them to say, "If this goes to a vote, we shall have to support the government," and then be free to go out on the hustings and say, "I could not do anything else. Those darn Tories and C.C.F.'ers in the house forced us."
Whatever has happened in this country with regard to our industrial and financial condition is due entirely to the lack of planning on the part of the government and to the fact that they have kept the people of Canada in ignorance of the true conditions. Therefore they must accept their responsibility, and the government members of the house will have to accept theirs as well.

I now return to the more serious material which I have before me. First, to give the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) a rest, if for no other reason, I should like to refer to the speech made last night by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson), and the one made this afternoon by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). Both of these hon. gentlemen referred to our United States neighbour in a way which I think was uncomplimentary, and which showed a want of knowledge of the United States and of our position with relation to her.
First, the hon. member for Mackenzie took it upon himself to criticize the United States because she emerged from the war strong and powerful. He held that that country should have used its resources for the common good in achieving victory. That remark will be found at page 581 of Hansard. That remark shows in particular, first, the want of knowledge of the capacity of that great country to the south of us. Had the hon. member seen what I saw during the war; had he known anything of the difficulty of fighting a war on two fronts; had he known anything of the unstinting help which the United States of America gave to all of its allies, including the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, for whom the C.C.F. show so much admiration; had he known of any of these things he could not have made the statement he did. I suppose it merely goes to prove that the socialists are merely bankrupt capitalists, and the greatest and most outstanding thing in their philosophy is an envy of those who can produce.
The United States economy has reached its present position and its strength, which I think a sensible man will admire, because for years and years, almost since their inception, the businessmen of the United States have been able to get a hearing before their senate and house of representatives. They have been able to go to Washington and show, as businessmen, how they could increase their production, employ more people, reduce costs and generally do things to benefit their own country; and in almost every instance they have had the help of their representatives in the house and in the senate. What do we find in Canada? We find Canada faced with an industrial revolution. Can businessmen come here to Ottawa- and tell the Minister of Finance their troubles?

If they come here and sit in the gallery what do they hear from the socialists to my left? They hear themselves blackened as capitalists, men who make a profit, when actually in this country wages have risen by a greater percentage than profits. They find themselves badgered by government; they find themselves regulated by investigators and they find themselves weighted by taxes. How can you produce in a country like Canada? We have the industry, the initiative, the foresight and the confident ability to plan, ability to fill these gaps in our own economy which are now being filled by imports from other countries, and the will and the desire to produce in order to better the standard of living of the Canadian people. How can the producers of this country find the courage, the initiative and the capital to go on when they are faced with this constant stream of envious criticism from socialists and communists alike?
We had in Toronto the other day a visitor who spoke to one of the union congresses, and he supported capitalism. He spoke before one of the same congresses that have lent their support entirely to the socialist party in Canada. His name was a Mr. Woll, a vicepresident of the American Federation of Labour. These unions which are non-communist led would do well to listen to him, because the unions and their leaders are in business. They need good working conditions; they need to see the industry in which they serve in a healthy condition. They need to be associated with a profitable enterprise, no matter what my socialist friends may say, because if an enterprise is profitable they will be justified in asking for wage increases and sharing in those profits.
It is just as simple as this. You cannot milk a starving cow, and if industry in Canada is not in a healthy condition the working people will suffer as they are suffering today under the present government embargoes. The condition we find in Canada at the present time is a pathetic one. One cannot deny the necessity of action to conserve United States exchange. One would certainly be ill advised or ignorant to try that. However, we can point out that the situation was foreseen and indicated clearly to the government. We can say that on July 5, 1946, the revaluation of the Canadian

We can regret that the government has taken the advice of the socialist-minded planners instead of calling to this capital practical men skilled not only in industry but in banking and exchange matters. I will go on later to say what I think they would have recommended.

I have already recommended that the Minister of Finance call to Ottawa some of those in this country who are skilled in the day to day fluctuation of exchange values, as well as in commerce and in the export and import business, and he might consult the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and the boards of trade.
I was going to say that in the United States they enjoy the benefit of examining exports and imports, and finance and industry before committees of the house of representatives and the senate; but when we tried to examine anything before committees of this house we are blanketed by a very cunning government policy. I have in mind, when I say that, the war assets committee, when we saw drained away into the dark comers of Canada great assets left by the armed forces of the country; assets which had been paid for dearly in taxation by the Canadian people and which were resold to them again at still higher prices.
Before I was distracted I was saying I would recommend that the government consider the policy of permitting the Canadian dollar to find its economic level in the exchanges of the world. He would be pleasantly surprised, I think, to find how much real support the Canadian dollar had, and I do not believe jit would initially fall much below ninety cents, although there might be a period of instability when it would fall below that. But if he freed it from his control at a pegged price I think he would do a great service to Canadian producers.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South says it is not an exchange crisis. I disagree with him on that statement. I feel it is

entirely an exchange crisis caused by the government's unrealistic approach to our postwar economy. Had they, perhaps eighteen months ago, started necessary restrictions through a tariff policy, which they certainly could have amended in any of the three budgets, to my mind they would have stopped the heavy imports of a great many of the capital goods and other goods into Canada which have so drained our resources of United States dollars.
Last session I received a great many complaints from producers in Canada. They all protested against the twenty-five per cent excise tax, particularly because the argument of the Minister of Finance against devaluation was that it would cause rising costs in Canada to the extent of perhaps ten per cent. I do not see how anyone in his right senses can argue that a ten per cent rise in costs in Canada is a bad thing when the Canadian consumer is faced with a twenty-five per cent rise in cost as a result of the excise tax.

This afternoon the hon. member for Stan-stead (Mr. Hackett) mentioned how controls of this nature begot further controls, until the whole of the economy is under the control of the government. We have a warning to that effect in Hansard at page 539, a warning from no less a person than the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), where he says:
So far as the government is concerned this would have the advantage of allowing the Minister of Finance a little more time for the preparation of further measures he will have to bring on later.
We see the words, "Further measures he will have to bring on later"-more controls, more bedevilment of the industry of Canada. Now we have seen the results of government interference with industry. We have seen it with particular clarity in respect of the gold mines. Once the government placed its withering hand on the gold mines of Canada, their future became more and more obscure; and the government has so discouraged this great dollar-earning industry that it is producing at less than half of its capacity. The government has denied it a free market. Why? Because the government wants to control that industry. It wants to control gold just as it wants to control industry.
The government has tied Canadian gold mining to the international monetary fund, a fund which received its first blow on Saturday, when the French republic devalued the franc and became a realistic trader in the world's export markets.
The gold mines are also harassed by the government's taxation measures, which are so stringent that they have caused as much as twenty per cent absenteeism in some parts of the country. This absenteeism results from inhuman taxation methods. In 1939 an exemption of SI,000 was allowed a working man, and $2,000 to him if he was married. With the purchasing power of the dollar forty per cent depreciated, that $1,000 should now become $1,400 for the single working man and $2,800 for the married man. But what is it in reality? With an exemption of $750, and a forty per cent depreciated purchasing

Foreign Exchange Conservation
power, the working man today starts to pay taxes at the $450 level when compared with 1939 standards.
Taking 1939 as the basis, the married man starts to pay a tax when he has reached the equivalent of the $900 level. We have there a difference between a real exemption of $1,400, as it should be at present day rates, and an exemption of only $450, for the single working man.
This excessive taxation gives rise to many social problems. All the veterans are concerned. Those who are married are being miserably squeezed. This condition comes right down to the administration of rent control when we see the rentals administrator ruling in favour of veterans and penalizing landlords so that they may help the veterans over this difficult period. We see these boys and girls piling up debts, and developing friction in their home lives. They are faced with tremendous rising living costs. The working man and his family are suffering equally. He has had to curtail purchases of food; his clothing budget is reduced, as are his budgets for recreation and cultural interests. At the same time his fear of unemployment is greater because high taxes make it impossible for him to save.
Turning to the situation in France, Great Britain, Sweden and other trading countries of the world we see them thwarted by the Bretton Woods and Dumbarton Oaks agreements, which pegged currency values at the end of the war. No account was then taken of the tremendous readjustment of currency values which must inevitably follow the destruction in Europe. Their theory was that there should be rigid control of capital and money. However, at considerable cost to the Canadian people the government has learned that it cannot control the commodities it sought to control. Capital and money are notoriously timid and invisible and they will move in spite of regulations and will therefore be impossible to regulate.
I predict that the government will be unable to enforce its currency restrictions, that the dollar will continue to be traded at around ninety cents or possibly less on the free market and that eventually England will have to follow France's move and devalue the pound in order to export. I predict that the government's planners when confronted with the present situation will prove inadequate to their task. I should like to ask the Minister of Finance a question.

He has had from Saturday to consider the effects of the devaluation of the franc and he should have in mind some course of action which should be followed by this country to keep us from the worst effects of a currency debacle. That is what we are headed for. This currency debacle is being brought about by the policies of the international monetary fund. Those policies have been unrealistic. The currencies of all countries in the trading world, with the exception of Switzerland, have been overvalued in terms of United States dollars. This over-valuation makes it impossible for some countries to export to the United States and it makes it difficult for others to do the same thing.
What has brought about this situation? It is caused by the fact that a nation's money and credit find their true reflection in the exchange markets of the world. That reflection in the exchange markets of the world is a direct result of the particular government's monetary policy. The most, influential thing in setting the value of a country's currency in the markets of the world is the government's policy. If that policy is inflationary, then the money of that country will be cheap. If the policy is a stable one, then, that country will find it easy to trade. If the policy is deflationary, then there will be a demand for that currency and its value will rise on the exchange markets of the world.
I wish to emphasize that this valuation is influenced by the government's monetary policy. It can also be influenced substantially by the productivity of a country, the quality and quantity of the goods produced and the demand for those products in other countries. But I repeat that the most important thing is the financial policies of the government in office. The government has had one answer to its financial policy. The government went to the United States and was told that it was a good risk for only $300,000,000. That poor credit results directly from the course on which the government has guided this country since the end of world war II.
The international bank has been a brake on world trade. They have undervalued the United States dollar and have hindered exports by other countries to the United States. In some cases the effect has been to add as much as 100 per cent to the Smoot-Hawley tariff. Nobody can sell to them under conditions such as that. If we wish world trade to survive, and I am sure we all do, we must first have realistic currency values and then the removal of artificial barriers and controls. We may then find that

other countries will be content to lower their tariffs and thus create a more stable trading economy.
When I commenced my remarks I said that I would1 make certain recommendations to the government. I make them now in goodi faith. I recommend that the government call in immediately the exchange experts from the banks and exchanges of Canada and hear their views, in private if necessary but preferably in public, on the present inflationary monetary policy being followed by the government. I would recommend that with the inauguration of the price spreads committee we should institute an exchange probe. These practical men have the knowledge to deal with the socialist planners who are now advising the government and they would be able to teach them some of the principles of international monetary exchange.
I think the government should withdraw the bill at this point and permit the Canadian dollar to find its own level in the free market. If necessary they should amend the tariff in order to stem the tide of excessive imports.
In closing I invite hon, members of the Liberal party who are true Liberals to stand up and declare themselves on this measure. I invite them to stand up and be counted because I know that those who are real Liberals will vote against the bill.
