ROSS (St, Paul's): Mr. Speaker, I sympathize with the minister and his colleagues for the predicament in which they find themselves, but perhaps I should not because they have only themselves to blame for having got into this mess, and it really is a mess. I wonder if hon. members realize that when the government believes it is in the best interests of its own policies it may pass any order it pleases with regard to trade, regardless of the legislation which parliament itself has enacted or may enact? Do hon. members realize that this bill gives the government the power to prohibit absolutely the importation of goods from another country which the government may allege it is in the public interest to prohibit? This parliament is to

part with its right to say what is to be imported. As I have said, the effort is to get away from parliament altogether.
Let me pause and ask my hon. friends who support this legislation whether they believe in the old principle of no taxation without representation.
They accuse our party of standing for certain principles and Shibboleths. Well, if we stand for them, we stand for them because they have been the security of men and nations through the centuries and they are the things that have stood up against revolution and against the kind of movements hon. gentlemen-the C.C.F.-are fomenting at the present time.
I appeal to horn, members on this last opportunity they will have of recording where they stand on these great fundamental principles to forget their party prejudices and show by their votes that they regard as more essential than all else the proper parliamentary proceedings in all matters pertaining to the control of taxation and expenditure by the people's representatives in parliament, and that they regard as more sacred than all else the maintenance of the constitution of the country and of all that constitutional government seeks to secure.
I have borrowed these words with a few changes. They are not mine, but they seem to be very appropriate to the present occasion, and that is the appeal which I now make. The government has, of course, power now to prohibit the export of goods from this countiy and is using that power in banning the export, for instance, of cattle. The words I have quoted were the words of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King); and I can think of no better way of appealing to my hon. friends opposite than by having just quoted them, if they believe in the principles of freedom, liberty of the individual and of free enterprise. I think the Prime Minister and his colleagues in the cabinet have forgotten what he called fundamental principles. Those principles seem to have disappeared from the Liberal platform these days. The Liberal party seems to me, and is, we know, a party which, if anything goes wrong, at once resorts to a little more regimentation, putting a few more controls on. They have not the courage of their convictions to stand up for these principles but are interfering with business all the time. It seems to me that that appeal which the Prime Minister himself made should be sufficient to convince hon. gentlemen opposite. It was spoken under the difficulties which beseiged the government of that day.
I suggest that the members on the other side of the house stand up and show by (heir votes

that parliament is supreme and that they do not intend to delegate these extraordinary and arbitrary powers to the discretion of any one person. Let them show that they still stand for the principles of freedom, free enterprise and liberty of the_ individual, and that they believe in the right of the citizen to recourse to the courts. How strange it is that the Prime Minister should have held those principles then and that he holds the principles that he does today! It is just a right-about face. Scant attention has been paid to the principles which he held out to his party for so long and which the public had been led to believe were the mainstay of his party.
One of the difficulties with this administration is that they cannot get used to parliamentary control. They have had a free hand for so long and they are still war-minded. They refuse to let the laws of economics work. The sooner we get back to those laws, the better it will be for Canada and the less we shall suffer in the long run.
This bill takes away from parliament its supremacy. That is one reason why I do not like it. Another reason is that it will regiment the people. Another reason is that it will mean the creation- of another large body of people to administer the act. At the present time business does not know where it stands or where it is going. That condition needs to be remedied and remedied at once.
I know of one man who wanted to bring in some goods from Great Britain. He went over to Great Britain and spent quite a lot of money in preliminary arrangements, and then this austerity program came in. Since he did not have any imports before July 1, he could not get a quota, even though, as I said, he had already spent a considerable amount of money. It is true that the goods he was going to bring in were more or less luxury goods, greeting cards, for instance, but greeting cards in Great Britain are a high-class article that we should be glad to have, -but he is prohibited from bringing them in. We shall see further about that when we get into committee.
Another reason why I do not like this bill is this. No sooner had it been announced to the public that seventeen countries had cooperated and agreed to lower tariffs on January 1 of this year than Canada made use of the escape clause in the treaty right away, just like that, and the Minister of Finance announced his austerity program nullifying all these concessions. It does seem to me that that is not quite playing the game with these other countries.
I do not know why the dollar was revalued upwards some time ago. Perhaps the government became a little afraid of the tremendous
buying that was being done by the people of the United States in Canada and thought it might lead to a shortage of goods here. The minister talks about why we cannot devalue the dollar. As a matter of fact, I cannot see any particular reason why the dollar was revalued upwards when our dollar was worth only ninety cents and is still worth only ninety cents. However, it was revalued upwards. At the same time that the dollar was revalued upwards we did have a good deal of buying by United States customers in this -country of ordinary staple goods of one kind and another which brought in United States dollars. We have lost these dollars. We also had an incentive to the tourist trade. These incentives are largely gone.
The minister talks about what the effect of devaluing the dollar would be, or what the effect was when it was at ninety cents. He said that the cost of living would be increased. It would be increased a little bit but not very much. He said that it would be ten per cent across the board. That is not so. It would be ten per cent only on the wholesale price of the goods in the United States plus ten per cent on the freight to the Canadian border, but that does make a lot of difference. ' Most of the goods in the bureau of statistics cost of living index are Canadian. The minister said at page 91 of Hansard:
When that action was taken in June of 1946 I do not recall that the leader of the opposition or any member of the Progressive Conservative party rose in his place to object to it.
I do not think anybody did rise in his place to object to it. If they did I do not recollect it; but when that action was taken nobody in this House of Commons knew the exact position of Canada with respect to United States dollars. I recollect plainly that on many occasions the amount of United States exchange which the foreign exchange control board had was asked for by certain people and it was always kept a dark secret.

It would permit people to pick and choose for themselves. It would permit people still to retain their freedom; it would permit parliament to have freedom as well instead of being dictated to. It would sell more goods to the United States; it would bring in more tourist dollars. In that regard may I refer to what the people of northern Ontario had to say on the subject, as quoted in the Ottawa Journal of January 26 (C.P.):
Ontario's tourist trade will suffer severe reverses unless the Canadian dollar returns to the $1.10 premium over United States money, Len Hughes, director of the Northern Ontario Outfitters' Association told delegates at their annual three-day convention here today.
That is the opinion of a gentleman who knows something about the subject. In addition to that, we would get ten per cent more for our newsprint, our copper, our gold, our lead and other commodities. It would make a market in the United States for goods where we have not one now. It would increase the Canadian production of all goods, and amongst the others things it would increase the United States investment in Canada.
I turn now to the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), development, reconstruction and supply, radio, transport and austerity. At page 385 of Hansard he is reported as having said:
We devalued the dollar in 1910 as a means of meeting a situation that would have seriously impaired our ability to fight a war.
Further on he said that we could not revalue the Canadian dollar because it did not do any good. He contradicts himself in these two statements. In the first place, he said it was a good thing to devalue the Canadian dollar for war purposes, and later on he said we could not do it now because it would make everything too expensive, and so forth. He contradicts himself when he says that. Then, when he is asked how long it will take to get our exchange in good shape he answered the question by saying, "I do not know; it will take some months." When he is asked if it will take three or four months he says, "It will take some months." When he is asked, "Will it be soon?" he says, "I do not know." Then again he says, as reported at page 385 of Hansard:
I said I was basing my opinion on my experience, and my experience was that from the time
the dollar crisis appeared in 1941, the situation had been corrected in about nine months' time.
It was corrected in about nine months by the devaluation of the dollar at that time. If it could have been corrected in nine months by the devaluation of the dollar at that time, it seems to me that that is the proper method to use at this time. The minister also said at page 386 of Hansard-.
I might say a word about the "dictator" charge which hon. gentlemen opposite love to make.
Well, we do not love to make that remark about the minister, but there is no getting away from the fact that that is what he is. If he does not like it he should not accept the position. He makes the regulations or laws; he enforces them; he hears the appeals; he adjudicates on them and his decision is final. I do not know what a dictator is if that is not one. It seems to me that is what he is; and yet, with all that, the minister calls himself a Liberal. We hate to have to call him a dictator, we hate to have to call anyone in parliament a dictator; but the government decided they would have a dictator, and they think he is the best man for the job. The minister gives lip service to free enterprise, believes in competition, and dislikes regimentation; yet he condones this bill and takes on the job of dictator, which is the very antithesis of free enterprise and freedom.
Some time ago it was suggested in this house by many of us that we should have a moratorium on the building in Canada of projects which were not absolutely necessary, such as motion picture buildings and so on, the reason being that we wanted to have more materials and labour for other purposes, but the minister insisted that the federal controls could do nothing of this kind. That was when he dumped the responsibility for construction liabilities in the lap of the municipalities. They were to choose what should go up and what should not go up. He said that nothing could be done, and it is extraordinary that he takes the stand he does now in order to justify his sweeping powers. He says that much relief would be brought to housing and high priority industrial construction by the action which was being taken. In the meantime, twenty months have passed and nothing has been done with regard to having some priority on necessary buildings, and the cost of building has skyrocketed. All materials and labour are scarce and there is really too much building going on at the present time. That is one of the difficulties.
In October, 1946, when the government revalued the Canadian dollar to a par with the United States dollar, as you know, the Cana-

Foreign Exchange Conservation
dian dollar had been arbitrarily valued by the foreign exchange control board at ninety cents American. This step was taken in spite of many factors then known to the government. The quick economic recovery of Europe was then known to be wishful thinking. Canada was selling large quantities of goods to European countries for credit because our own economy required it, and still does, and we had previously made loans to those countries for that purpose, loans which were running out very much faster than had been anticipated; in fact, they had all been half used up.
The government also knew that we could expect very few United States dollars in payment for our goods from those countries. It was known that Canada had been expending her United States dollar store at an ever-increasing rate to buy goods in the United States. It was then expected that the Canadian adverse balance would amount to over half a billion dollars by the end of the year. It was plain common sense that one cannot go on for ever selling for credit and buying for cash, or one would run out of cash.
In spite of these facts and others, the government took the worst possible step to increase this adverse balance of payments by re-valuing the Canadian dollar. It wiped out the ten per cent discount; it took the brakes off Canadian buying in the United States. Various houses in Canada which had been wanting to buy for some time thought the green light had been given to them to go ahead, and they went ahead and bought all kinds of goods, necessary and unnecessary, in the United States market which accelerated the depletion of our store of United States dollars.
This had a manifold effect. It increased Canadian buying of United States goods and decreased United States buying of Canadian goods by eliminating the ten per cent incentive. It had a dampening effect on the tourist trade, as illustrated by the clipping I have read. The extent of the effect it had it is hard to say, but it is acknowledged that it had a great effect. It decreased the value of gold to Canadian mines by S3.50 for every ounce sold. It lost for Canadians $10 on every hundred pounds of goods sold in the United States, and those goods were those which the United States had to have. They could not do without them, goods such as newsprint and so on.
It reduced the movement of United States capital dollars to Canada by investment from some $280 million a year to a mere trickle. Canada paid in dividends to people in the United States, on balance, some $200 million more than we received. This accounted for the necessity of finding another $20,000,000.
At the end of 1946 our adverse balance with the United States was $600 million. The deple-5849-40
tion of our United States dollar store was accelerated. It was known in the early part of this year, while parliament was sitting, about May, to what extent the situation was worsening, and that some action would have to be taken. It was pretty well estimated by those who knew, and a great many others suspected, that Canada would have an adverse balance at the end of 1947 of about $600 million, and that our United States dollar resources would dwindle from $1,200 million at the end of 1946 to about $250 million at the end of 1947 and be entirely wiped out early in 1948 unless something were done.
The House of Commons was not so informed and no action was then taken, the excuse for not doing so being that it might upset some of the negotiations going on in Geneva in regard to world trade if the situation were disclosed. I might say that if the facts were not disclosed, then, to say the least, it was a lack of honesty on the part of the government in these negotiations. However, no action was taken until the situation was in an awful mess.
Then the government acted with its usual disregard for the supremacy of parliament. Three announcements were made on the same day. The Prime Minister sugar-coated the bitter pill of the Minister of Finance, followed by the speech of the newly created totalitarian minister, the Minister of Trade and Commerce. There was a wonderful new-era speech by the Prime Minister-everything was to be lovely-which was followed by the everything-not-so-nice, austerity speech of the Minister of Finance-not so good-I do not know how long it will be-and the usual optimistic one from the new dictator, the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I may say that if his foresight with respect to this austerity program is as good as with respect to housing, he should have said, "Prepare for a long time", because I think it will be a long time.
I know that in the beginning the development of the crisis was not all of the government's making, but this policy certainly aggravated it. So much for this brief review.
In announcing its program, the government has had an utter disregard for parliament. The far-reaching effect on the economy and liberty of the individual is unpredictable, but, if continued, will be severe.
Demands were made on the government some months ago to call parliament, but no heed was given to those demands. No doubt the government was afraid to face the angry voices of the members, hoping that the people would be lulled into complacency by hopes held out to them of trade agreements if parliament were called late enough in the year

Foreign Exchange Conservation
so that it could be gagged. That is exactly what 'happened. The government announced its austerity program on November 17. The Minister of Finance announced a budget while parliament was not sitting. For the first time in the history of any Canadian parliament a budget was announced while parliament was not sitting. Let me remind the house of what happened recently in Great Britain when, the Right Hon. Hugh Dalton was dismissed for giving information with regard to his budget before it was brought to the house. Never have I heard of such an outrageous proceeding or never have I known of a democratic government anywhere which imposed taxation such as has been done here by order in council without consultation with the House of Commons, and when the House of Commons was not sitting.
I think no more outrageous deception was ever perpetrated on the House of Commons than in the stand taken by the foreign exchange control board, with the knowledge and direction of the government, to use powers given to the government for certain purposes and with the assurances of the government to the House of Commons that those powers would be used only for the purposes indicated, only to find that on November 17, 1947, the powers thus secured were utilized under a pretence in order to effect the wielding of power which the board had never been intended to have. We have taxation without representation. The government has gone a long way in its transitional powers act to deny the individual the right of recourse to the courts.
I should like to remind the house that a few weeks ago, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, then Minister of Reconstruction, came back from Britain. He spoke in Toronto and in scathing tones condemned the socialist government of Great Britain for placing powers in the hands of one man. Now this government which pretends to be Liberal is asking parliament to place in his hands-and I might say in the hands of a man who has never had, to my way of thinking, a scrupulous regard for parliamentary procedure-power over every individual industry in this country; power in the words of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), to say to one industry, "You shall live"; to another, "You shall die"; to say to one industry, "You shall receive," and to another, "You shall be denied"; and no one who is affected is permitted access to the courts.
Mr. Speaker, where will freedom be when one individual in this country is given such powers as that? Our dollar is now worth

only eighty-five to ninety cents in United States funds at the present time. Why not deal with the matter in a courageous way, devalue the dollar and get our dollar value down to be worth what it is worth? It will not cost Great Britain as much to buy food.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are discussing a bill respecting emergency measures for the conservation of Canadian foreign exchange resources. It is true that we must conserve United States dollars; but reading through the present bill causes me to wonder if a synod of fiends, bent upon the complete ruination of Canada, could have drafted a worse bill.
It is rather important at this time, I think, that we as a House of Commons should ask ourselves what it is that has got us into the swamp of difficulties which impelled the government to adopt such extreme measures as are set forth in this bill. In the first place, I would say, in answer to that question, that it was just pure government foolhardiness in accepting unsound agreements. Hon. members will recall that in the fall of 1945 members of this group did everything in their power to bring the House of Commons and the country to realize the dangers of accepting Bretton Woods and also of accepting entangling trade agreements which it was quite evident were to follow upon Bretton Woods. The fundamental reason why we are in the trouble we are in tonight, and why we are considering this bill with all its objectionable features, is that we accepted Bretton Woods. There is not any way of explaining that away; and our Conservative and C.C.F. friends might just as well face up to that fact and assume the responsibility which it is fitting they should assume, because they supported the government in that exceedingly reckless and dangerous set of agreements called Bretton Woods. All of these agreements-Bretton Woods and the trade agreements which were considered in Geneva and are now, I understand, being studied at Havana-are centred around the principle of non-discrimination in trade. That sounds attractive but it is actually exceedingly pernicious. These agreements are also centred around the idea that debts

_______________Foreign Exchange Conservation
which result from adverse trade balances cannot be paid or cleared away with goods other than gold unless the creditor nation sees fit to accept the goods. It seems difficult to impress that fact upon all those who should be impressed. Nevertheless, what I have said is true.
There is another cause for the government's being in the difficulty it is now in and dragging the country through the mire, and that is the fallacious trade theories which have been entertained and advocated by the members of the government-which were not seriously objected to by the other parties except the Social Crediters-and false theories as to what constitutes a sound national economy. I have heard since 1935, when I first came to the house, the Prime Minister repeatedly declaim against what he called economic nationalism. The time he has used in condemning economic nationalism would make one think that it was the worst thing that could possibly be conceived, that it was the cause of wars, and of all the other wretchedness to which mankind has fallen heir. All economic nationalism means, in the last analysis, is national selfsufficiency. Imagine a government which for years has followed a policy which was opposed to economic nationalism, or national selfsufficiency !
That is the record of the Liberal party before this country for the last quarter century, and it shows how successful they have been in deluding the people of Canada when they have been elected time and again despite their policy, namely because the people of Canada were not informed.
This Liberal administration under the leadership of the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King has played a considerable part in ruining the Ottawa agreements, which were the great contribution made by the Conservative party under the leadership of the late Viscount Bennett. If the Liberal party could point to any achievement in all its long tenure of office which could compare with the Ottawa agreements, they would have much more to rejoice for than they have at the present time.
This same party, while tendering lip service to the idea of a greater and stronger British commonwealth, nurtured and defended by imperial preferences; this same party, while giving lip service to that general principle, has given me the impression that it has done a good deal toward destroying the British commonwealth, and the trade association which has existed among the members of the commonwealth, not so much by anything it says, as by the things it does, similar to the signing of these pernicious agreements to which I have already referred.
5849-40J
We are beginning to see the results of what they have done. There is not much use in finding fault. After all, the damage is done. What we should do is look to the future with the idea of altering our ways. There are things we can do about this situation, dark as it is. While I presume all the members of * the opposition will vote against this bill; all the members of the government will vote for it; the bill will pass-and away it will go, until they find force of circumstances rendering it impossible to follow the act. Then they will do something else.
It seems to me that it is the duty of every member in the house, and especially the duty of members of the government, to see if *they cannot work out a plan for the future, which will offer much more hope than anything we have had in the last year.
The first thing I would recommend is that this house, without further delay, take steps which are necessary to withdraw from Bretton Woods. They should give formal notice and then go through with it, just as soon as they possibly can, under the agreements we have; for the longer we stay under Bretton Woods, the worse our condition will become.
It will not do any good for me to rise in the house five years from now, if all goes well, and say, "I told you so." It will at that time be obvious to all, just as I said in 1945 it would be obvious in a few years, that Bretton Woods was fallacious. Let us see if we cannot be really worthy of the responsibilities resting upon our shoulders at the present time, and take the necessary measures. Let us give formal notice of our withdrawal from Bretton Woods and so give leadership to the other nations of the world, so that they can consider a similarly sound proposal.
It is evident that the Bretton Woods agreement is completely unsound and is being found unworkable. The measure France has had to take in spite of the monetary fund within the last two or three days, when she devalued her currency, is clear evidence that this pernicious Bretton Woods thing will not work. The nations will simply be crucified if they try to make it work.
The next thing we ought to do as soon as convenient to us, is to denounce the principle of non-discrimination in trade. Non-discrimination would not be objectionable if all nations were equal in economic power. But all nations are not equal in that power. The result is that to have large nations like the United States in a non-discrimination arrangement with small nations like Holland is absurd; just as absurd as it would be to have boys fifteen years old playing marbles in the same ring with boys six years old, and insisting upon the

Foreign Exchange Conservation

6-year-old boys following the same rules as are followed by those who are sixteen years old. No one in his right senses would favour that.
The present arrangement we aie seeking to establish among nations of the world is just as grotesque, absurd and unworkable. It means that the big boys like the United States will get everything and the small boys will reap destruction. Canada is beginning to see what can happen, with S900 million in adverse trade balance in one year. Heaven knows how we shall pay it back. Let us face that fact. And if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) would spend a little more time in figuring out how we can pay that back, instead of taking such a cocksure attitude, as though he knows all there is to be known, he would really discharge his responsibility to this country just a little more effectively than he is doing today. It is getting beyond a joke entirely.
The next thing we ought to do is to work out some method, by conference with the nations, whereby the nations which fall into [DOT]debt, as a result of adverse trade balances, may have some chance of clearing themselves out of it. That is, we should have some arrangement whereby creditor nations, which become creditor nations just as the United States is this year a creditor to the extent of $900 million with respect to Canada, through adverse trade balance, would be obliged to accept in return goods other than gold; for small nations like Canada are unable to pay enough in gold; yet they need to get out of debt.
How are we to get out of debt? If we fall into another adverse trade balance of $700 million next year, what shall we do with the resultant $1,600 million? Surely, as responsible members of the House of Commons we cannot permit this country to slide along as though we had no responsibility. Remember, the interests of our children and our children's children are at stake in this matter. These are real things we are talking about these days. So I would say that the third thing we have to do is to find some means whereby debts, which result from adverse trade balances, on account of inequality of productive potentials of nations participating in world trade, can be in some way or another repaid. If the Geneva trade conference, and trade conferences of that kind had worked on that problem they would have been really profitably occupied.
The fourth thing which, it seems to me, might be highly desirable is this: To devise and to adopt by agreement a measure Jo prevent industrial penetration of the weaker economies by the stronger economies. It is
[Mr Blackmore.]
manifest that the United States, with its tremendous population, can produce goods in great numbers. It can deliver them in Canada more cheaply than our industry can, when it serves a nation of only 12,000,000 people in competition with a nation of 140,000,000. I know that the cards are stacked against any industry in Canada which seeks to compete with a corresponding industry in the United States. What measures can be arrived at and agreed upon by the various member-states to prevent that industrial penetration whereby goods are obtruded into the markets of the weaker nation by the stronger nation, to the disadvantage of the industries of the weaker nation and the destruction of its employment structure? That problem must be solved.
If the wise men who met at Bretton Woods and Dumbarton Oaks, and I do not know how many other places during the war, and were planning to follow the advice of some little gang somewhere to destroy the peace and prosperity of the world entirely, had been busy on this problem, they would have been doing some work which would have been for the real benefit of the world.
There are some other things we in Canada can do, and in our own right. I hope this government has not given away our right to govern ourselves-although I am afraid they have done it. It seems they have given up the right or power to use subsidies to modify prices. If they have done that, we must agree they have pretty well given up all right our nation has to control its price structure. Apparently they have gone on and acted stupidly, failing to realize what they were doing. I do hope that there are still some things we can do within Canada.
If we have not bartered our freedom away, here are some of the things that we can do. We must realize that it is sound for us to work for national self-sufficiency. That principle was laid down this afternoon by several members and yesterday by several others. The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) pointed out the danger we are in with regard to coal and steel. How much better it would be if at the present time we knew that we were able to supply the coal needed throughout this dominion without worrying about the United States.
The same applies to gasoline. We simply must be more nationally self-sufficient. One thing which was done during the war and which will stand to the credit of the government, unless it weakens and gives it all up, was the building of a synthetic rubber plant at Sarnia. That was sound. If it is sound for rubber, it certainly is nationally sound for the other vital necessities of Canada. That ought

Foreign Exchange Conservation
to be clear to all. No more argument is necessary. Why does the government not go ahead with other vital needs?
Why did the government establish a synthetic rubber plant in order to make its own rubber and then persist in the stupid attitude it has adopted in connection with the beet sugar industry? We could be self-sufficient in sugar.

speechtext:
Someone says that we need private enterprise, but we did not need private enterprise in the case of the Sarnia plant. Private enterprise would take care of the beet sugar situation if the government would get off their backs. It does not see fit to do that.
In addition to rubber, one of our great needs in Canada is gasoline and oil. There are sufficiently large deposits of coal in Canada which could be processed to supply our requirements. The Germans showed us during the war how they could produce synthetic gasoline which enabled them to put up such a terrible fight. Sufficient gasoline could be produced from the coal in Alberta to supply the whole country of Canada. The necessary gasoline and fuel oil could be produced, as well as many other commodities, for centuries to come. Why should we import gasoline and oil from the United States and be in danger of facing the major calamity to which the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) referred this afternoon should the United States cut off our oil supplies? We could not blame them for doing that because they are in danger of suffering from a shortage there.
Why should we be in danger of a shortage of gasoline and oil when we have all the coal that is necessary to produce these commodities? During the war, I repeat, the Germans showed us how admirably they could process coal into gasoline and other commodities which were necessary to carry on the war. We can blame nothing but our own stupidity-

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Liberal stupidity.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
Yes, it is Liberal
stupidity in more ways than one. The coal in the Lethbridge area, which I represent, or in the area south of Calgary would provide sufficient supplies. Great pipes could be laid down, granted at tremendous cost but the investment would pay great dividends in the course of twenty-five years, to carry the oil, gas, and gasoline from Alberta to Ontario and Quebec. We could supply the two central
provinces with all the gasoline, fuel oil, diesel oil and natural gas and the like that they require.
Somebody will say that that is too grand a scheme, that it is too ambitious and costly. The people who have accomplished things in this world were those who could dream dreams, who had the courage to go ahead and make their dreams come true. Canada is capable of dreaming the dreams which are necessary; she has the energy and courage to make those dreams come true. We have the facilities here. God has taken care of that. It is for us to determine whether or not we are going to use them.
Those hon. members who have read the newspapers lately will know that the United States is intending to build processing plants for the production of synthetic gasoline. Interior Secretary Krug proposed to the government of the United States on January 26 that they spend $9 billion on synthetic oil projects. If the United States is getting into a position where it must consider measures of that sort, a country which has a great deal of gasoline, what ought Canada to be doing when our production, as the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply said this afternoon, is only about eleven per cent of our needs? Our needs are extensive and they are going to increase. They will become imperative because we are in an age wherein we require gasoline to carry on our way of life.
I do not wish to labour over-much the beet sugar question, but this matter is far more serious than we can get the minister to realize. Somebody should take him out into the back yard and deal with him long enough to get him to realize how serious this question is. There is no reason why we should be in danger of having to spend $28,000,000 of United States funds every year to obtain sugar. There is no reason why we should be in danger of being short of sugar should there be another war when we can produce all the sugar this dominion could possibly use, in Alberta in the area south of Calgary and still have plenty of room for vast production of other commodities.
If we do not use the means at our disposal it will be due to the stupidity of the government in power, or to the lack of vision on the part of the people of Canada in not putting the necessary pressure on the ministers to see that they do the things which they ought to do. What is the government going to do this year about the beet sugar industry? Last year the minister laid fine plans and we heard much about the great acreages of sugar
Foreign Exchange Conservation

6:n
beets that were to be planted. Then we saw the minister dawdling along, and there was delay for weeks and weeks and weeks when a vital decision should have been reached which would have enabled Canada to produce millions more pounds of sugar. The result was that Canada did not produce the beets she could have produced. There is only one man in Canada who can be blamed for that, the Minister of Finance.
If the Minister of Finance has not the power, he should tell the people why he has not. He should tell the people who is holding him down, who is preventing him from doing the sensible thing in regard to beet sugar. We are reaching the time when people are getting ready to plant beets. I wonder if we are to be treated to another dose of "consideration", "consideration" and "consideration" until it is too late to do what ought to be done. We want action in Canada. The people are entitled to action even if they are unfortunate enough to have elected a Liberal government.
Another matter which is not being adequately dealt with in Canada at the present time is our tourist trade. There ought to be a systematic handling of this problem. The tourist industry is one of the greatest industries in Canada at the present time and it could be greatly enlarged. One thing that is holding up this industry is our lack of roads. The central government has simply stayed out of the road picture and has left the provinces to take care of this matter. As affairs now stand, it is impossible for the provinces to deal adequately with their roads.
Take my own province of Alberta as an example. There are 90,000 miles of roads in that province; a tourist might want to travel over any one of those miles. But there are only 800,000 people to take care of those roads. The present administration in Alberta is doing a magnificent job in building roads, having spent $13,000,000 this year, but it simply cannot build roads fast enough to permit the tourists to come in and enjoy the beauties and wonders of Canada and give us the income which we could have from the tourist trade.
I urge the government to wake up and get to work on the tourist business while there is still an opportunity to cut down our great deficit of United States dollars by the revenues from that business. The government of Canada ought to take a definite interest in the construction of roads. It ought to call the provinces together and discuss with them the road problems of the various provinces and be prepared to pay one, two, three, four, five or six dollars for every dollar the provinces spend until such times as the roads are brought

into a condition where they will be inviting to the tourists. We should also help the provinces to maintain those roads.
It will be said by a number of people that that is not federal responsibility, Mr. Speaker, it is the responsibility of the ministers at Ottawa to help look after everything that pertains to the welfare of Canada. If the provinces are able to discharge their responsibilities, well and good. The provinces ought not to shirk any of their responsibilities. But where a project is beyond the strength of the provinces and needs to be done, certainly everybody has a right to expect that the dominion government will enter the picture and assist in attaining the objectives.
There is a great deal to be done in the matter of fish. Everyone knows that tourists like to go where there are fish. We have an abundance of lakes and streams; all that it is necessary to do is to replenish them with fish. It is beyond the powers of the provinces to do this adequately, but the dominion government working with the provinces could lay down plans which would adequately supply our streams with fish and thereby create a very great attraction for the tourists.
We could also do much in respect of game which we are not doing now. I shall not go into details, but once more it is a question of finance. We did not have a single bit of difficulty in raising billions when the war was on, and if we got into war again, within six months I am sure we would again be voting billions and billions for war. What is the matter with the mentality of a people who can raise billions for war but cannot raise millions for peace? It will be said that in the war we went into debt, but everybody who has taken the trouble to inform himself knows perfectly well that money can be obtained without debt and without taxation. The Minister of Finance knows that, if he would only acknowledge it instead of trying to bluff himself out of any offer to discuss money in this house.
Canada must do more than I have suggested. She must devise means whereby she can conserve her population. It is a disgrace to Canada that we are a sort of supply depot and training school for the United States. We give birth to the children here and educate them; then we let them go across to the United States. The United States has been taking the cream of our population for years and years, and she is now getting down to the two or three top layers of milk. Yet all the time we are suffering from lack of population. Is it because Canada cannot produce enough things to enable her people to enjoy a high standard of living? Of course it is not. We can pro-

_______________Foreign Exchange Conservation
duce the goods. Then why do we not do so? We must do something to make our country attractive to live in.
I would suggest among other things that one of the first things we ought to consider is that threadbare one, namely, a housing program. I suggest that we should have a housing program that will include the common man who lives in what Roosevelt called the submerged third' of the population. We have a submerged third in Canada just as they have in the United States. There is no reason why the ordinary man in that submerged third should not have a home. There is only one way in which this can be accomplished and that is to make the money available to him at a rate low enough and on terms which will enable him to keep his home. It is high time that something was done about that. We have talked enough; even the Liberal government has talked enough about it. Now it is time to produce results; we need the results. We do not want to wait until another election and then have the Liberals try to trick the people into voting them back into power to fool the people for another five years. Let us have a real housing program now.
Then purchasing power ought to be made available, corresponding with the production of goods in this country'. It is simply common sense to recognize that. Then w'hy is not something done to see that purchasing power does go into the hands of the people, so that the boys and girls who are growing up in this country can visualize possibilities in its future? We should have a price structure that will be kept equitable and stable, so that people will have confidence that they will be able to live and raise their families here. These two things can be done only by monetary measures. I shall not go into that at the moment, but we must do something to keep our young people here. We need them. We should be a much greater and more powerful nation than we are today if we had kept the people here who have been born and raised in Canada in the last fifty years. Why should we not even try to draw the best of the people of the United States over here by making our conditions so attractive that they will want to come here? About all that the ordinary citizen of the United States has to do now is to come across the border and get a feel of our temperature-I do not mean the climate but the temperature of our economic conditions-and back again he goes to his own country.
To accomplish these things I have been speaking of with respect to purchasing power
and prices, we must insist on the right to use subsidies. I view with great anxiety the remarks made by such ministers as the Minister of Finance to the effect that the government does not favour subsidies. The government has already committed itself to the principle of floor prices. I ask any man or woman in this house, how in the world can you maintain floor prices without subsidies when the world market price happens to be below the price at which you wish your commodities to be sold in Canada? You cannot maintain prices without subsidies; for this government to commit itself to the idea that it is not going to give subsidies is for it to give up all possibilities of governing this country economically as it ought to be governed.
People may say that we cannot raise by taxation all the money we need for subsidies. I am not contending we should. First, let us recognize that we must have subsidies, and then adopt those measures which will enable us to pay subsidies. We can produce the goods. Let us learn how to turn them into money. We must maintain the right to use subsidies and not barter our rights away by signing some silly trade agreement like the one at Havana or something of that sort. We must use those subsidies instead of yielding to trade conferences convened and perhaps dominated by the United States.
We must adopt measures which will conserve our natural resources. It is often argued by Liberal apologists that Canada must export goods. Why must we export more and more goods? We must export goods because Canada is mining her soil, taking the richness out of the soil in those wonderful square miles we have in the great prairie regions, depleting the soil which should be maintained for future generations. We are simply selling the goodness of the soil, and we imagine we are building prosperity. Any man from an agricultural constituency such as the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Sinnott) knows what I mean. We are mining our soil. We cannot go on like that and have a Canada worth having for our children. We must cease producing vast quantities of goods to be sent abroad, with nothing to come back to take their place. We must conserve our natural resources, and now is the time to think about it, not after they are gone.
Our fisheries are being depleted. We are not taking the necessary steps to replenish those waters. What sort of improvident people are we when we do things of that sort.
Our forests are being devastated all over the land. We could replace our forests as we use
Foreign Exchange Conservation

them. Germany has done that and many other European countries were forced to do it. Let us do it before it is too late.
So I say that we must maintain our resources, and I say it is the duty of every member to see to it that as much as possible is done in that direction. Some may say that it is a provincial responsibilty. We must adopt a different attitude. There are some matters with respect to which dominion and provincial responsibilities merge into one.
I have seen a most tragic attitude develop in this country. We hear a great many people sneer about the colonial attitude that once prevailed. The attitude which now seems to possess the Liberal party is so much lower than the colonial attitude that I marvel our French-Canadian friends can stand for it. The government have adopted an attitude of abject menial submission to Wall Street. Here they have been standing up fighting for fifty, sixty or seventy years for independence against Britain, and they just run and throw themselves at the feet and lick the dirt off the shoes of Wall Street. They are doing it right along and they do not seem to take any interest in it at all. I wonder whether they cannot realize that there is a real power in Wall Street that may actually destroy their liberties far more than any power that ever came from Europe. I wonder whether they cannot be spurred with a desire to do something about this. What are the men of the Liberal party full of? Is there not somebody in the Liberal party who has vision, who has honour and courage and public spirit and patriotism and1 those other things, that will make them wake up and start doing something for Canada?
We should maintain a "greater Canada" attitude; we should adopt a "greater British commonwealth" attitude and do it right now, and1 stop thinking defeat. I hope I am wrong but, as far as I can see, the government at the present time are "selling Canada down the river," to use an expression which is rather commonly used across the line. They are making Canadians hewers of wood and drawers of water for the United States. It is an amazing thing. We gave of our best blood; we gave of our treasure; we gave of our all to defend ourselves against Hitler, and right at the same time that we were doing that here was the United States calmly and sardonically planning to d'o the same thing for us that Hitler planned. We are submitting to what the 'United States is planning, while we fought against what Hitler was doing. What is the matter with the people of Canada? Is there no leadership in this parliament anywhere that wTe cannot see that? We submit to maga-

zine articles and newspaper articles being written by United States people talking about their taking over Canada, and we pay no attention to it. We are allowing people to come up here and address our service clubs on the advisability of our being taken over by the United States. What would we have done if Hitler had talked of a thing like that? It<s about time we stopped thinking defeat. If we have absolutely to surrender to- the United States, well, then, let the United States stand up in the guise of a world dictator, a world conqueror and let her receive the publicity which Hitler received. Let it be known that what she fought this war for was to take over the countries she was supposed to be defending. Let it be revealed. That is all I say, and let us know where we are. If the government i3 absolutely powerless because somebody across the line is putting pressure on it, why does it not let us know so that we can all realize where we are going instead of pretending to be governing this country now in the interests of Canada and the British empire, but yet actually governing it in the interests of the United States?
It looks to me as if this government is actually participating in the breaking up of the British commonwealth. I do not want to speak overmuch of the British commonwealth, but in these days we are in an age of great combinations. We do not get very far unless we are part of a great combination. There never in this world's history has been a combination as potentially great and powerful as the British commonwealth, and never has there been a combination with the splendid ideals and willingness to serve and to suffer to improve mankind as is to be found in the British commonwealth of nations. Then, why are we disregarding its glorious possibilities that our ancestors and providence have built up and thrust into our very hands? Is it not about time that everybody, even the people on the street, began to realize that in Canada and talk about it and began to do something about this wonderful British commonwealth, this wonderful treasure placed in our hands before the little gang across the line utterly destroy it, as they are aiming to do?
Surely it is bad enough to submit to their dictatorship, but actually to take part in the destruction process ourselves is beneath contempt. It is an utter disgrace to our ancestors that their descendants should be taking the action that is being taken in this parliament right now, and by a government that is supposed to be a Liberal government.
In closing, let me say, first of all, if we pass this bill let us go right to work to see that if possible we will not have such a disgraceful

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) tossed down the gauntlet to the backbenchers of the Liberal party and it is with great pleasure that I am picking it up. The hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Skey) also tossed down the gauntlet and to him I might say hie sum in corpore et in spiritu hie.
Mr. Speaker, Bill No. 3 is merely a means to an end, and I maintain that it is a justifiable means to that end. I believe that there is far more, talking on this bill than is absolutely necessary, inasmuch as we are dealing with the principle of it at the present time. As the bill plainly states, it has to do with emergency measures for the conservation of foreign exchange resources. The word "emergency" is an all-important word. That is the reason we are using these means to attain the end which is necessary, namely, to conserve United States dollars. If we do not have United States dollars we cannot spend United States dollars. Apparently a lot of people do not realize what a serious situation it would create in this country if we should run out of United States dollars.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Oh, yes, we do.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
The only way to keep from running out of United States dollars is to conserve them or to increase the flow into Canada, and that is exactly what Bill No. 3 intends to do.
I supported the Geneva trade treaties in December and still do. I think they are a great step forward. Some people think this bill is contradictory in its nature as applied to the Geneva trade agreements. True, for a short period it is. The Geneva trade agreements were arranged with the long-term view of increasing international trade. This is an emergency measure to conserve United States dollars for the present time, which we must do.
I did not come to parliament to win a popularity contest and just do what seemed to be popular. I came here to do my duty by my constituency. I shall not be popular with all my constituents, perhaps, in supporting this bill. You can never bring down a bill which will be popular with everybody, but I do think there are a great many of them who will see that I have done the right thing in doing what I consider is my absolute duty. They know I am in a position to realize that, and any criticism that there may be in
Shelburne-Yarmouth-CIare in so far as I am concerned can be cleared up quickly by explaining why we are doing this.
The majority of people to whom I have spoken realize that if we are to have United States dollars we must either increase the flow of those dollars into this country or conserve what we already have. This is very necessary legislation. There is no question about that.
As regards the argument that we are becoming subservient to the United States of America, I maintain that is just a whole lot of bosh. There is nothing else to it. We are not any more subservient to the United States of America today than we ever were, and we never will be. I regard them as amongst our best friends. They are our largest customer and we are their largest customer. I maintain that if we are to have a happy and prosperous world we must deal with all nations of the world in the same way. Here is a perfectly good example, and let us work with the example as best we can and not try to defame those people or say unnecessarily unkind words about them.
The United States of America have been very good to my people in Nova Scotia and to the people of the maritimes. As a matter of fact a great deal of our trade has been carried on with them, and had it not been for them we would have been in the doldrums long before now.
This, Mr. Speaker, is a practical problem and I do not Chink it should be dealt with in an abstract way. I would say the best thing to do is to pass the second reading as soon as we can and then discuss the various items. There may be some items that will need a lot of explaining and no doubt there will be. But we are dealing now with the principle and1 I say that the principle is the right one under the existing circumstances.
I will not take up more time now because I would rather see the time spent in committee. I do not want anyone to run away with the idea that Liberal backbenchers are refraining from speaking because they are afraid to speak or do not support the bill. They realize that their votes are what count. I was not going to speak because I thought that when I voted for something that was sufficient. But the gauntlet having been thrown down two or three times, I could not resist and therefore I have risen to speak on this occasion.
I would say to the Minister of Finance that there is one thing he might add to Bill No. 3, and that is that during the emergency period an excise tax be imposed upon the excess of verbosity in the majestic halls of the House of Commons at the present time.

speechtext: The best contribution we have had so far.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
Well, there is one thing I always admire about the Minister of Finance. When he really discovers he has no other course to follow he appeals for help, and this afternoon I thought his appeal to the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Skey) was rather pathetic, because, after all, I would say for his information that it is not the function of the opposition to determine the policy which should govern the country. It is the function and Ihe sole prerogative of the government to introduce policies which His Majesty's loyal opposition are free to criticize and to determine whether they consider the government is worthy of support. By the same token, the moment the government feel the same degree of frustration that is at present apparent in this country, they have the right to throw in the sponge and 'hand over to His Majesty's loyal opposition the right to form a government and to introduce into the House of Commons policies which would mean a great deal to the Canadian electorate and to Canadian industry.
As we grow older we probably become more and more conscious of the past and possibly we may be given to reminiscence. I have had a rather varied and unusual political career, as many hon. members know, and my memory goes back to the days when political slogans were the order of the day. I think of the time when I almost suscribed-indeed I was quite enthusiastic about it-to the slogan adopted in 1935 which said, "King or chaos''. Someone behind me says that now we have both.
Without any disrespect to the Prime Minister, (Mr. Mackenzie King), we certainly have the most chaotic condition that has ever existed in Canada. My experience dates back to over a number of years, because I have been prone to regard myself as an economist, as a student of political history, and have been most enthusiastic about the contributions that have been made by, and the progress that has been made under, various governments in this country; and this is the first time in my experience that a government has deliberately gone out of its way, for some unknown reason -reasons about which we may conjecture or

may have suspicion-to create in Canada the greatest pall of gloom and despair which has ever lain upon the country.
During those dark and dismal days of the great war I heard many memorable and commendable speeches on the air. I refer to such great personages as Mr. Churchill and Mr. Roosevelt, and I could also include the words of the Prime Minister when he sought to describe what he termed a new heaven and a new earth for the Canadian people. Well, the voice which originated in London describing the Geneva trade pacts was indeed a preview of what he no doubt intended to be a new heaven and a new earth.
It is said that everything has its opposite. We have the negative and positive poles in electricity, one necessary to the other, and we know the opposite to heaven. I will not labour that point, but the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) followed, and after he had concluded his address I think I can say-I do not know whether my language will be considered parliamentary or not-we have been in a hell of a mess ever since. No one has any sense of direction.
I would challenge any businessman in Canada today to say that he can plan for the future with any sense of confidence, or whether he knows the policy the government intends to introduce within the next twenty-four hours; and I would challenge any member of the government, including nay right hon. friend, (Mr. Howe), designated the new czar of industry, to say that he knows what he intends to do within the next twenty-four hours. There are so few things that industry can plan and carry on with some regard for the future, with a policy which the master minds themselves do not comprehend; for that great body of motivated power, industrial genius, ambition and enthusiasm has been set an intolerable task. How can anyone plan when he does not know what direction to pursue?
Let us examine for a few moments, in relation to this Bill No. 3. some of the objectives of the present administration. Just before I left my home in Owen Sound in December to attend the special session, a young war veteran telephoned me to sa>
that he had ordered an electric range-in fairness to the manufacturer I should not disclose the name. This range was $297. I said that seemed almost enough. "Yes," he said, "but they have advised me that the price will now be $367. What would you do?" I replied:	"If I were you I would
stand by a few days because I am sure that once parliament meets and the opposition has an opportunity to enlighten the adminis-

_______________Foreign Exchange Conservation
tration with respect to some of the things they are doing you may anticipate some degree of relief." I did not make any contribution at that time; but my hon. friends and colleagues did, and I was happy to have this man telephone me when I arrived home and tell me that he had saved the tax on that electric range.
But there were others who, having some confidence in a degree of stability in government, had purchased equipment such as electric ranges and other equipment which they might require; and I am wondering what provision has been made for them with respect to the refund of the tax which they paid in the interval when this government-* operating in a haze or a London fog, or goodness knows what persuaded them-sought to introduce measures which were ill conceived and not properly studied or considered, and which were afterwards changed and are being changed from day to day. If you can think of any industry in Canada or any individual who has any sense of direction or confidence in the future of this great country as long as this government is in power, Mr. Speaker, I should like to meet him. That is the reason why I think the opposition quite properly challenged the government to consult the 'last court of public opinion, the people of this country. I am not one of those fellows who are running around looking for an election; but I love my country, and I have arrived at the place where I am prepared to make any sacrifice which is necessary to return this great dominion to some degree of stability, where people will have some confidence.
I am not a newcomer to some of the things I shall say tonight, because two years ago I challenged the Minister of Justice (Mr. Usley), who was then Minister of Finance, to tel! me where the pressure came from which caused the government, over a week end, to put our Canadian currency at par with that of the United States. Being a newcomer to parliament and not realizing that it is necessary to obtain an answer, I let the minister smile it off and the smile was never put on Hansard. I have yet to learn where that pressure came from. It certainly did not come from any quarter of this House of Commons, but it happened quite deliberately. I want to say that, as a simple problem of elementary economics, before the Christmas recess the Minister of Finance sought to leave the impression with this house that, had our dollar remained at ninety cents, it would have been a more costly experiment because of the amount of goods we are importing from the United States of America. I obtained his attention to ask
him to make his comparison on balance; because it is unfair to assume that we would have spent as many dollars in the United States if our dollars were worth only ninety cents as we spent them when they were at par. And conversely it is reasonable to suppose that more United States dollars would have been spent in Canada had their dollars remained at $1.10 in purchasing power. Yet if the Minister of Finance can establish his argument that we would have spent the same amount of money, of course it would appear that parity was the proper move. But I challenge that statement.
Mr. Speaker, I want to say to you that, on the eve of our joining Bretton Woods, recognizing the fact that our currency would be accepted at the rate of exchange currently in effect and realizing that we had the right to devalue our currency ten per cent still further without even the consent of the international bank, it would have given them a leverage between a dollar and eighty-one cents. In other words, we could have depreciated to eighty-one cents without the consent of that bank had we gone in with the 90-cent dollar.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Why not ten cents?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
Because ten per cent of ninety is only nine cents. As I say, the problem is elementary. The minister's question convinces me that I was correct.
Let us consider the matter for a moment. Surely our approach to the future of our problems in Canada can be gauged somewhat by our experience in the past. Even though my hon. friends opposite may suggest that it was because of war activity and otherwise, we know that while we possessed a 90-cent dollar we built up a $1,600 million surplus of United States dollars; and then, as a result of being ill advised, when we adopted parity, those dollars were drained off to the extent of over a billion, and that within a brief period of time.
Let me suggest that, as long as the United States dollar remained the standard of value throughout the commercial world, we enjoyed an advantage, not only in our approach to United States markets, but in our approach to all the markets of the world. With her tremendous development of industries as a result of the war, producing far more than her limited population could begin to consume, Canada was seeking and was bound to seek outlets for her surplus products. But this government sought to put upon industry, agriculture, and upon every producer in this country, the greatest handicap they could possibly conceive of. They sought not only to restrict our purchasing power but to level our dollar so that the United States of America would have the advantage over our dollar in

Foreign Exchange Conservation
the markets of the world. And all the time, Mr. Speaker, it was merely a joke; because I want to tell you that when we sought to buy and redeem Canadian dollars at par in Canada, if you look at the financial sheet of any daily newspaper you will discover that we have been discounted as high as fifteen per cent in the markets of the United States. I am prepared to accept the word of those who are world traders, men who-and Canadians at that- through their initiative, foresightedness and a degree of confidence in the governments of the countries in which they are doing business, have expanded their industries.
One of our greatest traders, a Canadian by birth, is on record as saying that the moment you try to place an artificial structure on your dollar, you are trying to maintain an artificial price which will tax the resources of your nation. I had a good friend, a man who was a friend of this government, the late Hon. James Malcolm, one time minister of trade and commerce in a Liberal administration. I can remember that in 1932 he said to me, "The more you interfere with natural laws, the more difficult it will be to govern." Just as my hon. friend the member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) said this afternoon: The moment you begin to interfere with natural laws, just at that moment you must impose restrictions and regulations. One restriction leads to another; one regulation leads to another. That which we have valued so highly, our freedom of enterprise, our freedom of thought, our rights as individuals, is cast aside, and in its place we have a system of regulations.	_
With all due respect I do not think there is a man in the house, no matter how sincere or capable he may be, who can regulate and govern the economy of this nation, a man who can seek to obtain a balance of production here and at the same time a restriction of production there.
As a result of the contribution made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) following the address of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) from London, these restrictions were introduced. I can well understand why there is a degree of hesitancy and uncertainty among the followers of the present administration because Canada has been placed in an untenable position at a time when she stood on the threshold of the greatest economic development in industrial expansion in her whole long history.
What do we find today? I do not know whether I should say the Minister of Finance went hat in hand-usually I am one of those who must wear a hat, when outside anyway;

and possibly there is good reason for it-but it has been said, and I will ask him to deny it if I am wrong, that this is the first time in our long history that we have ever borrowed money from a foreign government. So he has established a precedent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: We have borrowed a lot of money from foreign countries, though.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
Oh, yes; you borrowed from individuals who had confidence in this country. But you could not find the same sources available today because, as my hon. friends have said, those individuals did not think we had good business administration in Canada at the present time. So only a government could afford to take the chance.
One of the things I am concerned about is our relationship with our friendly neighbour, and in that connection I ask myself some pertinent questions. With our huge resources and our immense country, are we today becoming dependent upon the economy of the United States of America? Are we to become slaves to the United States dollar? Those are questions which are properly asked because the time will soon come when the repayment of debts will be an important factor.
Here we have journeyed on along life's highwny, indicating to our people a degree of prosperity, with the admiration of our friends in the Social Credit group-I mean the C.C.F.; one must be very careful not to criticize where criticism is not warranted.
Our socialist friends have admired the government as it has journeyed along the path to totalitarianism, because it has suited them. They have said, "Look at the degree of prosperity Canada enjoyed through the management of industry by the government during the war." Perhaps very few of us have stopped long enough to think this out. We borrowed one-half of our prosperity. We have mortgaged the future. .1 have no objection to that; as a matter of fact, I like to think of myself as a student of monetary reform. But there is one thing I would say, and that is that those w'ho have benefited by the bloodshed, sweat and tears which guaranteed our future freedom can well afford to pay, in kind at least, in a material way, for the success and achievements of our armies in the field. I am offering no criticism of the method employed in financing the war; but I believe we could have accomplished a great deal more had we determined that it would require not only bloodshed, sweat and tears but the whole

Foreign Exchange Conservation
resourcefulness of the Canadian people to gain to the full the great reward won for us on the field of battle.
It seemed to me most unusual that we should lead a life of ease and security when that future had been so dearly bought. Surely the law of compensation is still working; surely there comes a time when we must pay. So we are going to pay. This year for the first time in the history of our country we have departed from our usual procedure and, as the first step in our unknown economic future, we have borrowed 8300 million from a foreign government when, in my opinion, the whole thing could have been adjusted by allowing the medium which we use to adjust our balance in exchange to seek its own level.
One thing we must remember, and that is *that there is now a degree of inflation in the United States. Is it not strange that that flood of inflation did not hit Canada in a marked degree until the 'Minister of Finance said, "No longer can you buy Canadian-made goods without paying an excise tax."
I come now to a pertinent point. We have heard our socialist friends talk about the excess profits tax. They seem to think it is extremely bad business for any industrial concern to build up a reserve with which to meet problems in the future. Apparently they would be better satisfied to have the employers and their thousands of employees living from hand to mouth in these enterprises which, under circumstances of that kind, might easily collapse and go to the wall. It is interesting to note that when they point to profits they always pick the most successful enterprises, and fail to give any reference to the trying experiences they have overcome. They say nothing about the enterprises which have failed where people have invested risk dollars and have been willing to take chances.
While the House of Commons will in the near future name a committee to investigate price spreads and profiteering, I suggest to the house that one of the first witnesses to be called before the committee should be the Minister of Finance himself. If there ever was a marked degree of profiteering, it exists right in this government today. They have had absolutely no regard for the money that they required to carry on the business of the nation. They budgeted for a surplus of $80,000,000 or $180,000,000, and now it is said they will have a surplus of hundreds of millions. I realize that for a government steeped in wartime traditions a million or a hundred million is neither here nor there, but it means
a great deal to the Canadian taxpayer. There is nothing in this world which would make for a greater incentive in production.
In my contribution to the budget debate last year I challenged the minister to budget for a deficit of a quarter of a billion dollars and show that he had confidence in the future of Canada. Had he budgeted for a deficit of a quarter of a billion, he would have been far closer to the mark than he is now. He budgeted for a surplus and now they have so much money they do not know what to do with it.
Taxation has become a vital factor. It makes a tremendous contribution to the degree of labour unrest in our industrial plants. The take-home pay is a great factor in the worker's life. One sure way to defeat inflation is to increase production. We have the productive capacity because our people are possessed of the resourcefulness and genius to make their full contribution. But unfortunately, as I have said, we have in office a government whose powers to restrict have outgrown their desire to have things done. The result is that industry is languishing. Our farmers have no sense of direction. They do not know what they should plant next spring. Harvest time will arrive as it did last year and the government will begin squirming and turning about and talking about what should be done after the product is out of the farmers' hands and in the large warehouses of Montreal and Toronto.

This parliament is being asked' to delegate certain powers. Someone mentioned elevators in Owen Sound. The present Minister of Reconstruction and Supply and fisheries and finance and several other portfolios-what is his present portfolio?
