subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: All planners.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
I expert that all people do a certain amount of planning. I always plan my affairs so that I can stand on my own feet and not lean on somebody else. That is one thing this government have encouraged the people of 'Canada to do, to lean upon someone else. They have encouraged this great body of citizenry to become leaners. They themselves are leaners. The Minister of Trade and Commerce made a statement in the press that Canada was in for great times, provided that the Marshall plan succeeds. Where are your plans if the Marshall plan does not succeed? You have no guarantee that it will succeed. I am not going to raise my voice in any way that might defeat the success of the Marshall plan because it is necessary for world recovery. I hope 'that those who are dealing with it in the United States will take a reasonably generous view. They must do that if they hope for the survival of their own security and of the particular form of government which guarantees their freedom.
There has never been that planning and leadership for which Canada is starving today. Government has been carried on at the administration level. Canada is seeking leadership; it is seeking someone who will give

us a sense of security in our planning and in our hopes for the future. If the minister had made his comparison on balance I would have been perfectly satisfied. I admit that it probably would not be easy to make a comparison on balance.
We have sought to bring into Canada tourists from the United States to spend their money here. The tourist industry is one of our greatest industries. Yet here we find the Canadian government restricting the travel of Canadians to the United States. It would have been far better if the Minister of Finance had charged them SI.10 for every United States dollar they bought and let them go wherever they liked. That is freedom. But no, he sought to restrict them. The people of the United States, realizing that our price level is lower than theirs, would have flocked to Canada if their dollar would have enabled them to buy $1.10 of Canadian goods, which are worth about S1.60 in the United States. We must remember that whatever the United States is doing about the dollar they consider that their dollar is worth a dollar in their own country, and they let the rest of the world determine what it is worth in their countries. I think that would be a very good position for Canada to take. It certainly would provide us with a terrific advantage when we seek to sell our goods in the markets of the world. The challenge today is to determine exactly where we stand. Never can I recall a period in Canada's history when there was so much confusion in the public mind-I say this kindly but deliberately-and so much uncertainty as exists among Canadians today. They have a feeling of frustration, a feeling of despair, a lack of confidence. A sense of confidence properly should come from the leadership which one looks for in the government of the nation, but no government will survive in Canada or enjoy the confidence of the Canadian people which tries to live on the record of its past and which has no conception of present-day problems. That is the position of the present administration. They are accepting advice from certain groups or individuals who are theorists, to begin with, with no practical knowledge of business. Take our gold mining industry-

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask one question of the hon. member for Grey North (Mr. Case). He said that the minister should listen to the voice of reason. Very good advice. But whose voice is it? Is it the voice of my hon. friend? Is it the voice of his leader? Is it the voice of the leader of the C.C.F. party? Is it the voice of the leader of the Social Credit party? Is it the voice of my colleague the hon. member for Beauharnois-Lapairie (Mr. Raymond), who is not here but who can speak from long distance? Whose voice is it, the voice of reason? I should like to know. The advice given by my hon. friend was not complete. He gave very good advice to the minister but he did not finish his sentence. Will he be good enough to say whose voice, according to him, is the voice of reason and logic?

speechtext: If my hon. friend is asking me a question I would say just a word in reply. The voice of reason is the collective voice of the Canadian people who value freedom and justice above anything else in the world.

speechtext:
There was once a great politician across the border who was offering one of the provinces of Canada for sale. A friend of mine saw and talked with him, when other Americans were present. Afterwards they asked: Has he power of attorney to sell a province of Canada? I would ask my hon. friend what power of attorney he has to speak on behalf of the people of Canada. I ask that question to be informed by him, because I listened to him with joy. He does not send one to sleep. He is lively. He is eloquent; he speaks well. He is interesting. But he does not finish his sentences. Why does he start so well and not finish? He made my mouth water. I was expecting some wisdom from him and he gave us only eloquence. The brain food he gave us did not have enough in it of the salt of wisdom, and therefore I am very sorry his speech was incomplete. I would
have listened to him much longer with great pleasure if he had finished his sentences and had told us whose is the voice of reason, or if he had read to us in full the power of attorney that he has from the Canadian people to speak on their behalf.

speechtext: Very clever.

speechtext: He at least speaks for Grey North.

One at a time and I can handle them all. I do not say that because I dislike my hon. friend the member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe); I like him. But what surprises me is that my hon. friends have discovered grounds for challenge recently. They have been thinking deeply about the problems of the day, and I should not be surprised if the hon. member for Grey North were chosen by his party to make the speech he did tonight because he was elected in the dying days of the war, and just because he was not here when the former leader of the Conservative party-before it was Progressive -used to say, "Don't worry; don't bother; let the war go on, and after the war yye will talk business." That is the language which was used in the house by Mr. Hanson. The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), who succeeded Mr. Hanson, had too much common sense to make the same speeches. At the time there was no language of wisdom; there was no voice of wisdom. The minds of all members of the house were distracted by propaganda.
Today I am not in the position of the hon. gentleman who has challenged the government on this bill. If I look into the past; if I look into what has happened during the war, I will tell my hon. friend because he was not here at the time, that there were protests against the financial policy of the government, and at the time the challenge was not against one party, it was against the whole house. The Conservative party have not the right to attack the government since they are sinners as well in that respect because they have not shown that they were imbued with any idea of Canadianism. They were imperialistic to the core; when we were talking within the language of reason, of common sense, nobody was listening to it, and we were attacked. We were abused; we were called isolationists just because we saw what is happening today.
What about the gift of the formidable amount of S450 million for the air training plan, and what have we got for that? We have got wrought-iron gates for the Trenton camp.

He may be remorseful-

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS

speechtext: I will say to the hon. member for London (Mr. Manross), who was the last interrupter, that at the time Mr. Bennett was prime minister he was a Liberal himself, a supporter of the government; but that is off the record.

speechtext: Now that Lord Bennett has been embalmed and buried properly, let us proceed with the discussion that we were on a moment ago, and with a little order. That is a Latin phrase which means, "always the same thing." My hon. friend has missed it, but it is an accurate translation.
We can remember what has been done; we can recall it, and it is precisely because it has been done that today the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has to go to Washington to get some money from the United States government to help Canada.
How much did we spend during the war for war purposes? We spent S30 billion, and the amount of $300 million is just one per cent of what we spent during the war while we were financing the sterling area. My hon. friends were all for the financing of the British or sterling area.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

They applaud. I see my genial friend from Simcoe over there. He is applauding. He is ready to start again. I

should like to know what is the feeling of the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe). I am sure that he will be for it again, for the financing of the sterling area. The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario has vanished. I think he has had enough of what I gave him, but if he comes back I will ask him if he thinks that it will be good and sound financial policy to finance the sterling area. Then there is my hon. friend from New Brunswick, the radiant colonel, the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks). I am sure that he will be for it; therefore, if they are still for the causes of death, how can they complain that the minister goes to Washington to borrow more money? They stood for the causes of the mess we are in-and they still stand for them. They are silent now, Mr. Speaker. They do not protest. We do not hear any banging of desks. There they are. They are silent. They have been tamed, and the only thing to do is to confront them with their past record to show the absurdity of the policies of the Tory party. I cannot help saying how indignant I feel when I hear these denunciations of the government's policy by men who would probably have done worse if they had been in power. It was on the suggestion and the recommendation of the former leader of the opposition, Mr. Hanson, at that time member for York-Sunbury, that the government went into such an extraordinary move, financially speaking.
What will be the future? The future will not change. In the future we shall have the same financial policy in this country, whether this government returns to power after the next election or whether there is any other government, so long as nobody has the guts to make a clean-up in the Department of Finance and in the Bank of Canada. Abolish it and get rid of all those wizards-and I say that ironically. When I used the word "wizard"-for those who do not understand Job-I was using irony to describe these cranks.
The financial policy of this country since Bennett came to power has been failure, and it still goes on. Do you remember, sir, that the governor of the Bank of Canada boasted of following the financial policy of Schaeht in Germany? Do you know that the foreign exchange control board has been conducted by the most dangerous man who was sitting on the board of the bank of international settlement? They try nation-wide schemes until they fall into international experiments.
I wonder what will be the effect of the eloquent speech made by the hon. member
for Grey North. He spoke very well, but if he was chosen by his party to speak tonight, it was, I am sure, because he was not a member of this house when Mr. Hanson was the leader of that party. I said that Mr. Hanson made bold recommendations and suggestions to the Liberal party, and I cannot understand how it is that the Liberal party has followed his advice. But the last men to blame the government for having followed 'the views expressed and suggestions made by Mr. Hanson should be those who belong to his party, and those who were in the house when he made those recommendations. And even if they were not in the house, those were the recommendations made in this house by the leader of the party who was the loud-speaker of Arthur Meighen, who has been so often chosen for a short period of time to give the Tory party the illusion that he was bringing them to victory.
That is a sad story. I regret 'that the Minister of Finance had to borrow S300 million from the United States. I believe that economically we should be just as free from the United States as we should be from the United Kingdom. There is no reason why, economically at least, Canada should not be the mistress of her destiny. But I will go a step farther and say that if it is impossible for Canada to be economically independent without being politically independent, Canada should certainly be politically independent. But we shall not be independent so long as there are procrastinating imperialists in all parties in the house, men who should be denounced because 'they cannot be good Canadians. And that's that.
I believe that the Minister of Finance is well gifted and I sympathize with him because he has inherited an onerous legacy. But the legacy was not the 'tremendous debt of this country. It was not the taxes, which are a burden on each Canadian citizen. The legacy is the staff of the Department of Finance, the staff of the Bank of Canada, the staff of the foreign exchange control board, that octopus which creates ruin and danger, which creates disorder in this country.
If the hon. member for Grey North would listen to the voice of reason he would realize that reform is impossible in this country unless we return to the time when the minister of finance was boss of the Department of Finance and had to listen to false advice, wrong advice given by those wizards I mentioned a moment ago. There was a time when we had responsible government in this country, and the gold and securities belonging to the Dominion of Canada were kept in the east

Foreign Exchange Conservation
block where the Prime Minister has his office, where the council sits, where the Minister of Finance also has his office. They were the guardians of the public treasury. When I saw armoured trucks moving those securities to the vault of the Bank of Canada I realized that the time of ministerial responsibility had gone and that we would be in the hands of men who are incapable and incompetent. I do not want to go to the trouble of naming them, but everyone knows whom I mean, and it is not a question of being unpleasant to this one or that one.
The financial policy of the government has been unsound since these men have been put there. They have destroyed the wealth of Canadians in many ways by reducing the interest on deposits in banks and by doing all sorts of things that made people more miserable, that affected their wealth, things that may bring communism to this country in the near future.
How does communism arise? It comes when the people are deprived of their own property. I believe in the right of ownership, and the right of ownership is in accordance with the natural law. Is there a party bold enough to come and make definite recommendations for reform? What we need now is not at all what was mentioned a moment ago, namely leadership. What we need is reform. But we shall have no reform so long as we have irresponsible government in this country. I am ready to support the Minister of Finance to the limit if he is ready to make a house-cleaning in his department and to superannuate those men who cannot give sound advice to this country.
I have spoken of my hon. friends of the Conservative party. They procrastinate. They do not change. They are always the same. That is inevitable. But amongst the members of the party there are some good men; and I will mention two who helped me. I see the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol), an old sage, one of the best-informed members of the house. When I mentioned here that amounts below $25,000,000 did not appear in the public accounts, he rose and said it was an outrage. I relied upon his support and I relied also on the support of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) who helped me. At times I have obtained some support also from some friends in 'the C.C.F. group, from some friends in the Social Credit group and from some friends in the Liberal party. We tried to give an opportunity to the government to listen to the voice of reason.

Those men in the Bank of Canada, in the foreign exchange control- board and the other accessories are not the ones who will run before the people in an election. It will be the members of this house who will do that. When we go before the people, each one of us will- be asked what he has done to improve conditions in this country. If we bring about reform; if we see that we have responsible government in this party and that the financial policy is no longer imposed on the government by those men who were put in key positions by Bennett and who are still there, then the Canadian people will have a breathing spell and will be given relief. They will realize that we shall return to the good old times of Jim 'Robb, Fielding and also of White, who was a sound Minister of Finance.

speechtext: Why do you keep them in power?

Well, Fielding is dead,
Robb is dead and Sir Thomas White must be eighty-five years old. My hon. friend knows him better than I do.

speechtext: You are a supporter of the government. You are responsible for keeping the employees. You could dismiss them if you do not like them.

speechtext:
At the time there was no distinction between the financial policy of the parties except on tariff and regarding responsible government. The policy of the Conservative party at the time of Borden was the same as that of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and there was no change until Bennett came. When I was elected a member of parliament for the first time I felt at home in the House of Commons. I could follow the government blindly. I trusted them. But as soon as Bennett came in with that smart set, I could not do that, and I had to keep my eyes wide open. That is my answer to my hon. friend.
Before closing, Mr. Speaker, I wish to tell you one more thing. Some people have a feeling of joy to have forecast something. My feeling is one of regret. During the war, during the post-war period and even in 1946 when nearly all the members who are here tonight were members of this house, when I spoke of the fallacy of the loan gifts I was not listened to. I said to myself, is it worth trying to speak the language not of reason but of plain common sense to the House of Commons? I was not sure if I was right or if the majority composed of all parties was right. So I decided to stop speaking in the house for some time and to call on the English-speaking people of Canada in Ontario and in the maritimes to

find out what their reaction was. I found from those who were reading Hansard, not from those who were reading the English press- because with very few exceptions the English press of Canada is far from being informative about dominion affairs-that the stand which had been taken by a small group of members was supported by them. We were encouraged to go on to try to open the eyes of all.
This is said without any party bias. I respect my colleagues. They may differ with me, but they will realize at least that I have been consistent; and I regret deeply and profoundly that matters have grown much worse than anyone expected them to be at the time. Theoretical discussion about this bill will not bring any improvement to the financial policy of the government. I urge upon my most respected colleagues of all parties the necessity to realize that the time has come for reform. That reform will not be to go ahead with more crazy ideas. The reform will be simply and honestly to do at first an act of modesty, to realize that we must get out of that foolish
atmosphere created by wizards and return to responsible government, the responsible government which made this country prosperous at the time of'Macdonald, Laurier, Borden and Mackenzie King also until 1930. Let us make a general clean-up in the Department of Finance. Then it will not be necessaiy any longer to borrow money from the United States or from any other country.
